Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat.
She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.”
A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms.
If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins.
“I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said.
California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election.
The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections.
However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions.
The “weak gazelle”
Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman.
In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 27 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes.
Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax.
“We’ve identified that weak gazelle, the slowest gazelle, the one with the limp,” he said. “And that’s Josh Newman, in Orange County.”
Why Newman? Because he was elected by the slimmest margin of any senator, fewer than 2,500 votes.
In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax.
Close to 60% of voters chose to recall Newman in June 2018, replacing him with Republican Ling Ling Chang. The recall ended the Democrats’ supermajority in the state Senate.
In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy.
“If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said.
But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911.
In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.”
Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill.
“I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.”
Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5.
Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change.
How would it work?
If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election.
If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election.
If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change.
“The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said.
He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections.
However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort.
“It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.”
A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.”
Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions.

California's Proposition 5 would remove the "replacement vote" after a governor is recalled; here's who would take charge
Prop 5, a constitutional amendment from former state Sen. Josh Newman, removes question two from state recall ballots. Governors would be succeeded by the lieutenant governor; other vacancies filled by appointment or special election. PPIC has it losing 35% to 59%.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 12, 2026

California recall elections are changing under Proposition 5, which asks voters in November 2026 to remove the replacement question from state recall ballots.
Proposition 5 would rewrite how California recalls state officials. Today a recall ballot asks two questions: whether to remove the officer and, if so, who should replace them, with the replacement chosen by plurality from a list that ran to 135 names in 2003 and 46 in 2021. Prop 5 removes the second question (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/). A recalled governor would be succeeded by the lieutenant governor; other recalled statewide officers would be replaced by the governor's appointment; recalled legislators would be replaced through a later special election. It is a legislative constitutional amendment, SCA 1 by former state Sen. Josh Newman, who was himself recalled in 2018, and it is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/). It also has the weakest polling on the ballot: 35% yes to 59% no in PPIC's September survey.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California’s November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure’s rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The case for the measure is majority rule. Under the current system a replacement can take office with far less than half the vote, and in 2018 Newman's replacement won the seat with 31.8% of the votes cast on the recall question, fewer than voted to keep him. The case against is voter choice: opponents say Prop 5 "takes away half" of the recall right by giving the replacement decision to "Sacramento political insiders." This explainer sets out what the amendment's text changes, the recall law it amends, what the state's 11 qualified recalls since 1913 show, what the Legislative Analyst's Office says it would cost, and where the campaigns, parties and polls stand with three weeks to go.

In 2021, Gavin Newsom survived an effortto recall him amid the COVID-19 pandemic (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-08-26/2021-california-recall-election-guide). Voter guide to the 2026 California general election (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide)
Oct. 1, 2026
The basics
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time. Proposition 5 breaks up that process into two parts, prioritizing the voters’ right to oust an official before selecting a replacement.
The impact
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to change the current recall system. Under the proposed changes, voters would first be asked to choose whether or not to oust an official. Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date. In the case of a special election, the former officeholder could run again.
Advertisement
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.

Proposition 5 rewrites three sections of the California Constitution
The text of proposed law (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) amends Article II, sections 15 and 17, and Article V, section 10. It changes no statute directly. Its edits are short:
Section 15(a) strikes the words "and, if appropriate, to elect a successor" from the description of a recall election, leaving an election "to determine whether to recall an officer."
Section 15(c) strikes the sentence that makes "the candidate who receives a plurality" the successor, and strikes the ban on the targeted officer being a candidate. In their place it provides that if the majority votes to recall, "the officer is removed and the office shall be vacant. The vacancy shall be filled in accordance with this Constitution and statute, provided that the officer who was the subject of the recall election shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office."
Article V, section 10(b) is new. If the Governor is removed by recall, "the Lieutenant Governor shall become Governor for the remainder of the unexpired term," unless the recall comes "before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the Governor's term." In that case "a special election shall be called to replace the Governor," consolidated with the statewide primary; a candidate with a majority at the primary takes office, and otherwise "the top two vote-getters shall compete in a special election consolidated with the subsequent statewide general election."
Section 17 moves the job of running a governor's recall from the lieutenant governor, who would now be the successor, to the secretary of state, with the controller taking over if the governor and secretary of state are targeted at the same time.
The Attorney General's ballot label calls it a change for "statewide officers," but the text applies to every state officer subject to recall, and the LAO's analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm) describes its effect on Senate and Assembly seats as well. Prop 5 does not change how a recall qualifies, how quickly the election is held, or how local recalls work.
California recall law today: 12% of the last vote, two questions, a plurality winner
The power to recall is in Article II (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2014.&article=II) of the Constitution: "Recall is the power of the electors to remove an elective officer." A recall of a statewide officer needs signatures equal to 12% of the last vote for the office, including 1% of the last vote in each of five counties; senators, Assembly members, Board of Equalization members and appellate and trial judges need 20%. Proponents have 160 days to gather them, and the "sufficiency of reason is not reviewable." Once signatures are certified, the election is held 60 to 80 days later, or within 180 days to coincide with a regular election. An officer who survives is reimbursed for recall expenses, and no new recall can begin for six months.
The successor rule sits in section 15(c), last amended by Proposition 183 in 1994: if the majority votes to recall, "the officer is removed and, if there is a candidate, the candidate who receives a plurality is the successor. The officer may not be a candidate." Elections Code section 11385 repeats it: the candidate "receiving the highest number of votes for the office shall be declared elected for the unexpired term."
Prop 5 would replace that with the rules California already uses when an office falls vacant for any other reason. The lieutenant governor becomes governor under Article V, section 10 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=V). For the lieutenant governor, secretary of state, controller, treasurer, attorney general, superintendent of public instruction and Board of Equalization, Article V, section 5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%205.&article=V) has the governor nominate a replacement who takes office on confirmation by a majority of each house, or automatically if neither house acts within 90 days. For a legislative seat, Elections Code section 10703 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=10703) requires a special election "at least 126 days, but not more than 140 days" after the governor's proclamation, which must be issued within 14 days of the vacancy.
California has already made this change for local officials. Since January 1, 2023, under AB 2582 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB2582), recalls of local officers have asked only whether to remove the officer; under Elections Code section 11382 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=11382) the office "shall be vacant until it is filled according to law," and the recalled officer may not be appointed to the vacancy. Prop 5 uses the same structure and much of the same wording for state offices, which only a constitutional amendment can reach.
California recall elections are keeping their signature thresholds and timelines under Proposition 5 while the replacement question gives way to succession, appointment and special elections, as the measure's text and the California Constitution show in October 2026. The governor's seat under Prop 5: The lieutenant governor, then possibly a special election
For a recalled governor, Prop 5 creates a two-track rule keyed to timing. Late in a term, the lieutenant governor serves out the remainder, and no election is held for the seat until the next regular gubernatorial election. Early in a term, before the nomination period closes for the next statewide election during the governor's first two years, the lieutenant governor takes over and a special election is held alongside the next statewide primary. A majority winner there serves the rest of the term; without one, the top two meet again on the November ballot. The LAO's summary: the lieutenant governor "serves as Governor until voters elect a new Governor at a future statewide election" in the first case and "for the rest of the term" in the second.
Because Prop 5 removes the constitutional bar on the recalled officer's candidacy, a governor recalled early in a term could appear in that special election. The same applies to a recalled legislator in the special election that would fill the seat. The only limit the text adds is on appointment: a recalled officer "shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office."
That provision is the one even the measure's author has not defended. Newman told the San Francisco Chronicle's editorial board he could not explain why it is there: "I'm honestly not sure," he said (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-5-recall-california-22458510.php). "It wouldn't pain me if it wasn't there." The Yes campaign's website (https://fixtherecall.com/) presents it as a feature, saying that today's process "locks the recalled official out of the race entirely" and that under Prop 5 "the seat goes to a special election where every candidate can run." That description fits legislative seats and an early-term governor recall; for a governor recalled late in a term and for other statewide offices, the text provides succession or appointment, not an election.
California recall history: 182 attempts, 11 elections, six removals since 1913
The Secretary of State counts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) 182 attempts to recall state officials since 1913, 57 of them against governors. Eleven qualified for the ballot: nine against legislators and two against governors. Six succeeded: Senators Marshall Black (1913) and Edwin Grant (1914), Assembly members Paul Horcher (1994) and Doris Allen (1995), Governor Gray Davis (2003) and Senator Josh Newman (2018). No state recall effort is in circulation now, according to the Secretary of State's current-efforts page (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/current-recall-efforts).
The three most recent recalls show what the replacement question does. In 2003 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2003-special/sum.pdf), 55.4% voted to recall Davis, and Arnold Schwarzenegger won the replacement contest with 4,206,284 votes, 48.6% of the votes for a candidate and more than the 4,007,783 cast to keep Davis. In 2018 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2018-primary/sov/15-state-senator-29th-district.pdf), 58.1% voted to recall Newman in the 29th Senate District, and Republican Ling Ling Chang won the seat with 50,215 votes, 33.8% of the replacement vote and 15,982 fewer than the 66,197 cast for Newman to stay. In 2021 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/11-sov-summary.pdf), 61.9% voted against recalling Governor Newsom; the leading replacement candidate, Larry Elder, received 3,563,867 votes, which would have made him governor with 27.8% of the votes cast on the recall question had the recall passed. That is the "about 28%" figure in the Yes argument.
California recall results are showing replacement winners at 46.8% and 31.8% of the recall vote in 2003 and 2018, and 27.8% for 2021's leading candidate, in Secretary of State data compiled in October 2026. California is one of seven states that choose a successor on the same ballot as the recall, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures' survey (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials) of the 19 states that allow recall of state officials. Five others hold a separate special election and eight fill the vacancy by appointment, with some states mixing methods by office. Other reform ideas have taken different routes: the state's Little Hoover Commission recommended (https://lhc.ca.gov/press-release-43/) in 2022 a "snap" election in which "the targeted official is placed on the ballot with all potential replacements," plus a statewide signature threshold of 10% of registered voters. Prop 5 adopts neither.
Prop 5's cost: Savings or costs "in the range of millions of dollars," depending on the recall
The LAO's fiscal estimate (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm) is "unknown," because it depends on how often recalls happen and which offices they target. Removing the second question would save money on ballots and voter materials when no follow-up election is needed, which is the case for a governor recalled late in a term and for offices filled by appointment. A legislative recall would cost more if the follow-up special election "could not be consolidated with a scheduled election," at "millions of dollars per election." The LAO puts the net effect at "savings or costs potentially in the range of millions of dollars," less than 0.1% of the General Fund.
For scale, the Department of Finance's July 1, 2021 letter (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2021-recall/dof-allocation-costs-letter.pdf) estimated $243.6 million for counties and $32.4 million for the Secretary of State, $276 million in all, of which the Legislature appropriated $250.2 million; the same letter estimated $90.6 million if the recall had been consolidated with a regular election. Prop 5 does not change the cost of the recall election itself, only of what follows it.
Proposition 5's author and the vote in the Legislature
Newman, a Fullerton Democrat, introduced SCA 1 in January 2023. It passed the Senate 31–7 on February 1, 2024 and, after amendment, the Assembly 59–17 on August 30, 2024; the Senate concurred 32–8 the next day, and it was filed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) with the Secretary of State on September 10, 2024, directed to this November's ballot. Constitutional amendments need two-thirds of each house. The Chronicle's editorial board notes that Newman was recalled in 2018, won the seat back in 2020 and lost again in 2024. Of the 2018 recall, which his opponents tie to his vote to raise gas taxes, he told CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-proposition-5-explainer/): "I didn't do anything other than cast a tough vote."
Nobody is spending money on the measure. The Secretary of State's contribution page (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-5-sca-1-newman-elections-recall-state-officers-res-ch-204-2024) for Prop 5 reports "No committees identified" on either side as of October 6, and no Prop 5 committee appears on the FPPC's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), which covers committees that have raised $1 million. The Yes campaign's website is paid for by Californians For a Prosperous Golden State, the committee listed with Newman as the ballot contact. No opposition contact is listed in the Voter Information Guide.
The arguments: Majority rule versus the voters' pick
The Yes argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by the League of Women Voters of California, California Common Cause and former FPPC chair Dan Schnur, says the two questions together create "a dangerous loophole": "An elected official can be removed by a narrow majority. Then, a candidate listed in question #2 can win the office with far less than 50% of the votes cast." It cites the 2021 recall's cost as "more than $200 million" and says Prop 5 would stop recalls being used "to 'redo' an election as a political or partisan scheme." The Department of Finance's figures above support the cost claim; the 28% figure matches the Statement of Vote.
The No argument, signed by Senate Minority Leader Brian Jones and Assemblymember Joe Patterson, says Prop 5 "will take away your voice" because "politicians themselves—not voters—would choose who fills the vacancy" in many cases, and other seats "would sit vacant until another costly election." It objects that "that failed politician you just ran out the door… they'd be allowed to run in that next election," and its rebuttal says the author wants to change the rules after being recalled "when he raised taxes after breaking campaign promises." Carl DeMaio, the Prop 39 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/yes-voter-id-laws-are-on-the-california-ballot-proposition-39s-rules-costs-and-court-fights/) proponent, told CalMatters voters could be "without a representative for months, if not longer." Proposition 5 rewrites three sections of the California Constitution
The text of proposed law (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) amends Article II, sections 15 and 17, and Article V, section 10. It changes no statute directly. Its edits are short:
Section 15(a) strikes the words "and, if appropriate, to elect a successor" from the description of a recall election, leaving an election "to determine whether to recall an officer."
Section 15(c) strikes the sentence that makes "the candidate who receives a plurality" the successor, and strikes the ban on the targeted officer being a candidate. In their place it provides that if the majority votes to recall, "the officer is removed and the office shall be vacant. The vacancy shall be filled in accordance with this Constitution and statute, provided that the officer who was the subject of the recall election shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office."
Article V, section 10(b) is new. If the Governor is removed by recall, "the Lieutenant Governor shall become Governor for the remainder of the unexpired term," unless the recall comes "before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the Governor's term." In that case "a special election shall be called to replace the Governor," consolidated with the statewide primary; a candidate with a majority at the primary takes office, and otherwise "the top two vote-getters shall compete in a special election consolidated with the subsequent statewide general election."
Section 17 moves the job of running a governor's recall from the lieutenant governor, who would now be the successor, to the secretary of state, with the controller taking over if the governor and secretary of state are targeted at the same time.
The Attorney General's ballot label calls it a change for "statewide officers," but the text applies to every state officer subject to recall, and the LAO's analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm) describes its effect on Senate and Assembly seats as well. Prop 5 does not change how a recall qualifies, how quickly the election is held, or how local recalls work.
California recall law today: 12% of the last vote, two questions, a plurality winner
The power to recall is in Article II (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2014.&article=II) of the Constitution: "Recall is the power of the electors to remove an elective officer." A recall of a statewide officer needs signatures equal to 12% of the last vote for the office, including 1% of the last vote in each of five counties; senators, Assembly members, Board of Equalization members and appellate and trial judges need 20%. Proponents have 160 days to gather them, and the "sufficiency of reason is not reviewable." Once signatures are certified, the election is held 60 to 80 days later, or within 180 days to coincide with a regular election. An officer who survives is reimbursed for recall expenses, and no new recall can begin for six months.
The successor rule sits in section 15(c), last amended by Proposition 183 in 1994: if the majority votes to recall, "the officer is removed and, if there is a candidate, the candidate who receives a plurality is the successor. The officer may not be a candidate." Elections Code section 11385 repeats it: the candidate "receiving the highest number of votes for the office shall be declared elected for the unexpired term."
Prop 5 would replace that with the rules California already uses when an office falls vacant for any other reason. The lieutenant governor becomes governor under Article V, section 10 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=V). For the lieutenant governor, secretary of state, controller, treasurer, attorney general, superintendent of public instruction and Board of Equalization, Article V, section 5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%205.&article=V) has the governor nominate a replacement who takes office on confirmation by a majority of each house, or automatically if neither house acts within 90 days. For a legislative seat, Elections Code section 10703 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=10703) requires a special election "at least 126 days, but not more than 140 days" after the governor's proclamation, which must be issued within 14 days of the vacancy.
California has already made this change for local officials. Since January 1, 2023, under AB 2582 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB2582), recalls of local officers have asked only whether to remove the officer; under Elections Code section 11382 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=11382) the office "shall be vacant until it is filled according to law," and the recalled officer may not be appointed to the vacancy. Prop 5 uses the same structure and much of the same wording for state offices, which only a constitutional amendment can reach.
California recall elections are keeping their signature thresholds and timelines under Proposition 5 while the replacement question gives way to succession, appointment and special elections, as the measure's text and the California Constitution show in October 2026. The governor's seat under Prop 5: The lieutenant governor, then possibly a special election
For a recalled governor, Prop 5 creates a two-track rule keyed to timing. Late in a term, the lieutenant governor serves out the remainder, and no election is held for the seat until the next regular gubernatorial election. Early in a term, before the nomination period closes for the next statewide election during the governor's first two years, the lieutenant governor takes over and a special election is held alongside the next statewide primary. A majority winner there serves the rest of the term; without one, the top two meet again on the November ballot. The LAO's summary: the lieutenant governor "serves as Governor until voters elect a new Governor at a future statewide election" in the first case and "for the rest of the term" in the second.
Because Prop 5 removes the constitutional bar on the recalled officer's candidacy, a governor recalled early in a term could appear in that special election. The same applies to a recalled legislator in the special election that would fill the seat. The only limit the text adds is on appointment: a recalled officer "shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office."
That provision is the one even the measure's author has not defended. Newman told the San Francisco Chronicle's editorial board he could not explain why it is there: "I'm honestly not sure," he said (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-5-recall-california-22458510.php). "It wouldn't pain me if it wasn't there." The Yes campaign's website (https://fixtherecall.com/) presents it as a feature, saying that today's process "locks the recalled official out of the race entirely" and that under Prop 5 "the seat goes to a special election where every candidate can run." That description fits legislative seats and an early-term governor recall; for a governor recalled late in a term and for other statewide offices, the text provides succession or appointment, not an election.
California recall history: 182 attempts, 11 elections, six removals since 1913
The Secretary of State counts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) 182 attempts to recall state officials since 1913, 57 of them against governors. Eleven qualified for the ballot: nine against legislators and two against governors. Six succeeded: Senators Marshall Black (1913) and Edwin Grant (1914), Assembly members Paul Horcher (1994) and Doris Allen (1995), Governor Gray Davis (2003) and Senator Josh Newman (2018). No state recall effort is in circulation now, according to the Secretary of State's current-efforts page (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/current-recall-efforts).
The three most recent recalls show what the replacement question does. In 2003 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2003-special/sum.pdf), 55.4% voted to recall Davis, and Arnold Schwarzenegger won the replacement contest with 4,206,284 votes, 48.6% of the votes for a candidate and more than the 4,007,783 cast to keep Davis. In 2018 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2018-primary/sov/15-state-senator-29th-district.pdf), 58.1% voted to recall Newman in the 29th Senate District, and Republican Ling Ling Chang won the seat with 50,215 votes, 33.8% of the replacement vote and 15,982 fewer than the 66,197 cast for Newman to stay. In 2021 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/11-sov-summary.pdf), 61.9% voted against recalling Governor Newsom; the leading replacement candidate, Larry Elder, received 3,563,867 votes, which would have made him governor with 27.8% of the votes cast on the recall question had the recall passed. That is the "about 28%" figure in the Yes argument.
California recall results are showing replacement winners at 46.8% and 31.8% of the recall vote in 2003 and 2018, and 27.8% for 2021's leading candidate, in Secretary of State data compiled in October 2026. California is one of seven states that choose a successor on the same ballot as the recall, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures' survey (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials) of the 19 states that allow recall of state officials. Five others hold a separate special election and eight fill the vacancy by appointment, with some states mixing methods by office. Other reform ideas have taken different routes: the state's Little Hoover Commission recommended (https://lhc.ca.gov/press-release-43/) in 2022 a "snap" election in which "the targeted official is placed on the ballot with all potential replacements," plus a statewide signature threshold of 10% of registered voters. Prop 5 adopts neither.
Prop 5's cost: Savings or costs "in the range of millions of dollars," depending on the recall
The LAO's fiscal estimate (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm) is "unknown," because it depends on how often recalls happen and which offices they target. Removing the second question would save money on ballots and voter materials when no follow-up election is needed, which is the case for a governor recalled late in a term and for offices filled by appointment. A legislative recall would cost more if the follow-up special election "could not be consolidated with a scheduled election," at "millions of dollars per election." The LAO puts the net effect at "savings or costs potentially in the range of millions of dollars," less than 0.1% of the General Fund.
For scale, the Department of Finance's July 1, 2021 letter (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2021-recall/dof-allocation-costs-letter.pdf) estimated $243.6 million for counties and $32.4 million for the Secretary of State, $276 million in all, of which the Legislature appropriated $250.2 million; the same letter estimated $90.6 million if the recall had been consolidated with a regular election. Prop 5 does not change the cost of the recall election itself, only of what follows it.
Proposition 5's author and the vote in the Legislature
Newman, a Fullerton Democrat, introduced SCA 1 in January 2023. It passed the Senate 31–7 on February 1, 2024 and, after amendment, the Assembly 59–17 on August 30, 2024; the Senate concurred 32–8 the next day, and it was filed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) with the Secretary of State on September 10, 2024, directed to this November's ballot. Constitutional amendments need two-thirds of each house. The Chronicle's editorial board notes that Newman was recalled in 2018, won the seat back in 2020 and lost again in 2024. Of the 2018 recall, which his opponents tie to his vote to raise gas taxes, he told CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-proposition-5-explainer/): "I didn't do anything other than cast a tough vote."
Nobody is spending money on the measure. The Secretary of State's contribution page (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-5-sca-1-newman-elections-recall-state-officers-res-ch-204-2024) for Prop 5 reports "No committees identified" on either side as of October 6, and no Prop 5 committee appears on the FPPC's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), which covers committees that have raised $1 million. The Yes campaign's website is paid for by Californians For a Prosperous Golden State, the committee listed with Newman as the ballot contact. No opposition contact is listed in the Voter Information Guide.
The arguments: Majority rule versus the voters' pick
The Yes argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by the League of Women Voters of California, California Common Cause and former FPPC chair Dan Schnur, says the two questions together create "a dangerous loophole": "An elected official can be removed by a narrow majority. Then, a candidate listed in question #2 can win the office with far less than 50% of the votes cast." It cites the 2021 recall's cost as "more than $200 million" and says Prop 5 would stop recalls being used "to 'redo' an election as a political or partisan scheme." The Department of Finance's figures above support the cost claim; the 28% figure matches the Statement of Vote.
The No argument, signed by Senate Minority Leader Brian Jones and Assemblymember Joe Patterson, says Prop 5 "will take away your voice" because "politicians themselves—not voters—would choose who fills the vacancy" in many cases, and other seats "would sit vacant until another costly election." Then I'm weighing the "majority rule" point, since Schwarzenegger's 48.6% of the replacement vote still amounted to more votes than the 4,007,783 cast to keep Davis.

I'm weighing the "majority rule" point across the three recalls: in 2003 Schwarzenegger's replacement vote edged past the number who wanted to keep Davis, while in 2018 and 2021 the replacement winners fell well short of the No votes. The 2003 case is weaker since he still won under half of the replacement vote.

I'm working through how Prop 5 would have applied in 2003: since the recall came in Davis's first two years of his second term, a special election would have been consolidated with the March 2004 primary, with Lt. Gov. Bustamante serving in the interim, a Democrat, which would have meant a Democratic governor for that stretch.

I'm considering whether Prop 5's "first two years" window applies to Davis's 2003 recall, which fell in his second term's early stretch. Then I'm checking the 2021 case, where Newsom was in his third year, so the rule would have sent the Lt. Gov. to finish the term.

I'm checking whether Prop 5's "later in the term" wording would send the Lieutenant Governor through January 2023, and what happens to the 2022 election if that's the case.

I'm now weighing how the Prop 5 scenario would have played out in 2021: Lt. Gov. Kounalakis, a Democrat, would have taken over, so the voters would never have chosen the replacement. Supporters of the recall would call that a failure of majority rule, while opponents would argue that the voters' choice was already made by keeping Newsom.

I'm now checking how the replacement for other statewide offices would work under Prop 5: the governor would nominate someone, and that appointee would need majority confirmation in both houses of the Legislature, or would take effect automatically if neither house acted within 90 days. That somewhat undercuts the claim that Sacramento insiders would simply decide.

I'm checking the constitutional text on how the governor fills statewide vacancies, since the California Today guide says the nominee needs majority confirmation in each house or takes office after 90 days without action.

I'm checking the constitutional text on vacancy replacement next, since the Elections Code timing for a special election, the 126 to 140 day window, may matter for how quickly a consolidated election could fill the seat.

I'm moving on to check the editorial positions next, starting with the SF Chronicle and the McClatchy papers, to see whether they recommend No on Prop 5. I'm also planning to look at the state Democratic and Republican party endorsements, and at how Newsom has voted on the propositions.

I'm going to pull the rest of the California Today article and check the SF Chronicle and McClatchy editorials, plus the Democratic and Republican party endorsements on Prop 5.

Polling and endorsements on Proposition 5
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters, reading the ballot title "Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers," found 35% yes, 59% no and 5% undecided, the weakest position of any measure on the ballot. Opposition crossed party lines: Democrats 40% yes to 54% no, Republicans 34% to 64%, independents 28% to 65%. Asked which of the 14 measures interested them most, 1% named Prop 5. No other independent poll has published a Prop 5 result.
The parties split along legislative lines: the California Democratic Party supports (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) Prop 5 and the California Republican Party opposes (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) it. Governor Newsom, the target of the 2021 recall, plans to vote yes, according to the San Francisco Chronicle's account (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of the positions his campaign released on October 9. The editorial boards are divided. McClatchy's California board, writing for the Sacramento Bee and four other papers, endorsed (https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/proposition-5-could-change-california-173000601.html) it on September 18 because it "respects the democratic norm of majority rule." The San Francisco Chronicle's board recommended a no vote on October 8: it agreed "the second question is problematic" but called the provision letting recalled officials run again "a completely unnecessary provision" and "reason enough for voters to reject this measure."
Proposition 5 after November 3: A one-question recall from mid-December or the 1994 rule
If Prop 5 passes, it takes effect under Article XVIII, section 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII) on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote, which is due December 11. Any state recall after that would ask a single question, and the Elections Code sections that still describe a successor contest, such as section 11385, would sit under an amended Constitution that no longer provides for one. If it fails, state recalls keep the two-question ballot and plurality winner that section 15 has required since 1994, while local recalls continue under the one-question rule in place since 2023. Either way, the signature thresholds that decide how often Californians face a recall are not on this ballot.
This article reflects the Voter Information Guide as published, Secretary of State and FPPC campaign-finance data as of October 6, 2026, endorsements as of October 12, 2026, and polling fielded through September 10, 2026.

By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.

Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.

Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.

Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

Proposition 5 could change California’s recall elections. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Fri, September 18, 2026 at 5:30 PM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.
A volunteer with the Recall Gavin Newsom campaign collects signatures in Rancho Cordova on Jan. 23, 2021. On the election ballot this November, Proposition 5 will ask voters to consider changing how recall elections are held in California.
Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html) seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide. Such elections have been rare in California.
According to theLegislative Analyst's Office, (https://lao.ca.gov/) only 11 state recall efforts targeting nine legislators and two governors have qualified for the ballot since 1913. In 2003, Gray Davis (https://www.modbee.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/article251385288.html) became the only California governor to be recalled, a fate that also befell five state legislators over the years. The last statewide recall effort to qualify for the ballot was the unsuccessful campaign to oust Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/editorials/article253266413.html)
Under current law, voters are asked two questions in the same election when a recall effort qualifies for the ballot. The first is whether a state officer should be recalled. The second is who should replace that officer from a field of hopefuls seeking consideration if a recall is successful. In 2003, 135 candidates wanted to succeed Davis. In 2021, there were 46 candidates vying for Newsom's job.
THE BEE'S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html)
If Prop. 5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled. If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held. If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor. Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until a special election was held. If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that's more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It's why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop. 5.
Recall elections in California
Since California voters approved the recall process in 1911, five replacement candidates have been elected after six officials were removed from office with less than 50% of the vote. In California recall elections, the candidate who receives the most votes wins, unlike in a special election, where a candidate must win a majority.
Advertisement
Advertisement
This creates a conundrum of a recalled official garnering more voter support than the replacement candidate who "wins" the recall.
In the 2018 recall of former stateSen. Josh Newman, for instance, (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article145349124.html) his replacement, Republican Ling Ling Chang, came out on top with just under 34% of the vote. Newman points out that he had more votes in his favor; nearly 42% of voters opposed his recall.
"So I got more votes by way of 'no, don't kick him out,' than she got by 'yes, please put her in,'" Newman said.
Newman won back his Senate seat in the next regular election and then went on to write Prop. 5 (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-voters-prop-5-changes-recall-election-process/73175034).
One of the proposition's most outspoken opponents is Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a former talk radio host who pushed for Newman's recall in 2017.
How Prop. 5 opponents feel
DeMaio sees Prop. 5 as an attempt by the ruling party to evade recalls. "What they want to do is create a situation where politicians trying to fend off a recall can say, 'Don't vote for the recall or else you won't be represented for 12 months. You'll lose your voice,'" he told us.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Actually, Article II, Section 15 of the California Constitution, says a recall election must be held within 60 and 80 days of recall petition signatures being certified. The election may be held within 180 days of certification if it is consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election.
Arguments against Prop. 5 ignore that the current system created instances where replacement candidates got elected with less than 50% of the vote.
They decry the cost of conducting special elections and oppose that Prop. 5 would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the vacancy.
There have been 182 attempts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) to recall state officials in California. Eleven of those made the ballot, and only six were successful.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Some view the current recall system as "a weapon for political operators (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5.pdf) to undo election results they don't like," to quote the League of Women Voters and others.
Prop. 5 cannot put an end to the political gamesmanship, but it can safeguard the will of the voters by following the principle of majority rule.
McClatchy Media's California editorial board strongly urges a "yes" vote on Proposition 5.

Polling and endorsements on Proposition 5
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters, reading the ballot title "Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers," found 35% yes, 59% no and 5% undecided, the weakest position of any measure on the ballot. Opposition crossed party lines: Democrats 40% yes to 54% no, Republicans 34% to 64%, independents 28% to 65%. Asked which of the 14 measures interested them most, 1% named Prop 5. No other independent poll has published a Prop 5 result.
The parties split along legislative lines: the California Democratic Party supports (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) Prop 5 and the California Republican Party opposes (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) it. Governor Newsom, the target of the 2021 recall, plans to vote yes, according to the San Francisco Chronicle's account (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of the positions his campaign released on October 9. The editorial boards are divided. McClatchy's California board, writing for the Sacramento Bee and four other papers, endorsed (https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/proposition-5-could-change-california-173000601.html) it on September 18 because it "respects the democratic norm of majority rule." The San Francisco Chronicle's board recommended a no vote on October 8: it agreed "the second question is problematic" but called the provision letting recalled officials run again "a completely unnecessary provision" and "reason enough for voters to reject this measure."
Proposition 5 after November 3: A one-question recall from mid-December or the 1994 rule
If Prop 5 passes, it takes effect under Article XVIII, section 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII) on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote, which is due December 11. Any state recall after that would ask a single question, and the Elections Code sections that still describe a successor contest, such as section 11385, would sit under an amended Constitution that no longer provides for one. If it fails, state recalls keep the two-question ballot and plurality winner that section 15 has required since 1994, while local recalls continue under the one-question rule in place since 2023. Either way, the signature thresholds that decide how often Californians face a recall are not on this ballot.

Polling and endorsements on Proposition 5
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters, reading the ballot title "Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers," found 35% yes, 59% no and 5% undecided, the weakest position of any measure on the ballot. Opposition crossed party lines: Democrats 40% yes to 54% no, Republicans 34% to 64%, independents 28% to 65%. Asked which of the 14 measures interested them most, 1% named Prop 5. No other independent poll has published a Prop 5 result.
The parties split along legislative lines: the California Democratic Party supports (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) Prop 5 and the California Republican Party opposes (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) it. Governor Newsom, the target of the 2021 recall, plans to vote yes, according to the San Francisco Chronicle's account (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of the positions his campaign released on October 9. The editorial boards are divided. McClatchy's California board, writing for the Sacramento Bee and four other papers, endorsed (https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/proposition-5-could-change-california-173000601.html) it on September 18 because it "respects the democratic norm of majority rule." The San Francisco Chronicle's board recommended a no vote on October 8: it agreed "the second question is problematic" but called the provision letting recalled officials run again "a completely unnecessary provision" and "reason enough for voters to reject this measure."
Proposition 5 after November 3: A one-question recall from mid-December or the 1994 rule
If Prop 5 passes, it takes effect under Article XVIII, section 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII) on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote, which is due December 11. Any state recall after that would ask a single question, and the Elections Code sections that still describe a successor contest, such as section 11385, would sit under an amended Constitution that no longer provides for one. If it fails, state recalls keep the two-question ballot and plurality winner that section 15 has required since 1994, while local recalls continue under the one-question rule in place since 2023. Either way, the signature thresholds that decide how often Californians face a recall are not on this ballot.

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.

Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.

Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.

Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

Proposition 5 could change California’s recall elections. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Fri, September 18, 2026 at 5:30 PM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.
A volunteer with the Recall Gavin Newsom campaign collects signatures in Rancho Cordova on Jan. 23, 2021. On the election ballot this November, Proposition 5 will ask voters to consider changing how recall elections are held in California.
Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html) seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide. Such elections have been rare in California.
According to theLegislative Analyst's Office, (https://lao.ca.gov/) only 11 state recall efforts targeting nine legislators and two governors have qualified for the ballot since 1913. In 2003, Gray Davis (https://www.modbee.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/article251385288.html) became the only California governor to be recalled, a fate that also befell five state legislators over the years. The last statewide recall effort to qualify for the ballot was the unsuccessful campaign to oust Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/editorials/article253266413.html)
Under current law, voters are asked two questions in the same election when a recall effort qualifies for the ballot. The first is whether a state officer should be recalled. The second is who should replace that officer from a field of hopefuls seeking consideration if a recall is successful. In 2003, 135 candidates wanted to succeed Davis. In 2021, there were 46 candidates vying for Newsom's job.
THE BEE'S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html)
If Prop. 5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled. If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held. If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor. Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until a special election was held. If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that's more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It's why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop. 5.
Recall elections in California
Since California voters approved the recall process in 1911, five replacement candidates have been elected after six officials were removed from office with less than 50% of the vote. In California recall elections, the candidate who receives the most votes wins, unlike in a special election, where a candidate must win a majority.
Advertisement
Advertisement
This creates a conundrum of a recalled official garnering more voter support than the replacement candidate who "wins" the recall.
In the 2018 recall of former stateSen. Josh Newman, for instance, (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article145349124.html) his replacement, Republican Ling Ling Chang, came out on top with just under 34% of the vote. Newman points out that he had more votes in his favor; nearly 42% of voters opposed his recall.
"So I got more votes by way of 'no, don't kick him out,' than she got by 'yes, please put her in,'" Newman said.
Newman won back his Senate seat in the next regular election and then went on to write Prop. 5 (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-voters-prop-5-changes-recall-election-process/73175034).
One of the proposition's most outspoken opponents is Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a former talk radio host who pushed for Newman's recall in 2017.
How Prop. 5 opponents feel
DeMaio sees Prop. 5 as an attempt by the ruling party to evade recalls. "What they want to do is create a situation where politicians trying to fend off a recall can say, 'Don't vote for the recall or else you won't be represented for 12 months. You'll lose your voice,'" he told us.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Actually, Article II, Section 15 of the California Constitution, says a recall election must be held within 60 and 80 days of recall petition signatures being certified. The election may be held within 180 days of certification if it is consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election.
Arguments against Prop. 5 ignore that the current system created instances where replacement candidates got elected with less than 50% of the vote.
They decry the cost of conducting special elections and oppose that Prop. 5 would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the vacancy.
There have been 182 attempts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) to recall state officials in California. Eleven of those made the ballot, and only six were successful.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Some view the current recall system as "a weapon for political operators (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5.pdf) to undo election results they don't like," to quote the League of Women Voters and others.
Prop. 5 cannot put an end to the political gamesmanship, but it can safeguard the will of the voters by following the principle of majority rule.
McClatchy Media's California editorial board strongly urges a "yes" vote on Proposition 5.

I'm checking the recall figures from the California Today article against the SOS statements of vote, starting with the 2003 Davis recall, where the replacement vote totals and percentages need to line up.

I'm working out why the 2018 replacement figure differs between 33.8% and 31.8%: Chang's 50,215 votes against the roughly 158,000 recall-question ballots implied by the 58.1% and 41.9% split works out to about 31.8%, which would make the intro's number the consistent one.

I'm now checking the 2021 Elder figure: 3,563,867 votes is 27.8% of the votes cast on the recall question, which confirms the "28%" number from the statement of vote. Then I'm weighing the "majority rule" point, since Schwarzenegger's 48.6% of the replacement vote still amounted to more votes than the 4,007,783 cast to keep Davis.

I'm weighing the "majority rule" point across the three recalls: in 2003 Schwarzenegger's replacement vote edged past the number who wanted to keep Davis, while in 2018 and 2021 the replacement winners fell well short of the No votes. The 2003 case is weaker since he still won under half of the replacement vote.

I'm working through how Prop 5 would have applied in 2003: since the recall came in Davis's first two years of his second term, a special election would have been consolidated with the March 2004 primary, with Lt. Gov. Bustamante serving in the interim, a Democrat, which would have meant a Democratic governor for that stretch.

I'm considering whether Prop 5's "first two years" window applies to Davis's 2003 recall, which fell in his second term's early stretch. Then I'm checking the 2021 case, where Newsom was in his third year, so the rule would have sent the Lt. Gov. to finish the term.

I'm checking whether Prop 5's "later in the term" wording would send the Lieutenant Governor through January 2023, and what happens to the 2022 election if that's the case.

I'm now weighing how the Prop 5 scenario would have played out in 2021: Lt. Gov. Kounalakis, a Democrat, would have taken over, so the voters would never have chosen the replacement. Supporters of the recall would call that a failure of majority rule, while opponents would argue that the voters' choice was already made by keeping Newsom.

I'm now checking how the replacement for other statewide offices would work under Prop 5: the governor would nominate someone, and that appointee would need majority confirmation in both houses of the Legislature, or would take effect automatically if neither house acted within 90 days. That somewhat undercuts the claim that Sacramento insiders would simply decide.

I'm checking the constitutional text on how the governor fills statewide vacancies, since the California Today guide says the nominee needs majority confirmation in each house or takes office after 90 days without action.

I'm checking the constitutional text on vacancy replacement next, since the Elections Code timing for a special election, the 126 to 140 day window, may matter for how quickly a consolidated election could fill the seat.

I'm moving on to check the editorial positions next, starting with the SF Chronicle and the McClatchy papers, to see whether they recommend No on Prop 5. I'm also planning to look at the state Democratic and Republican party endorsements, and at how Newsom has voted on the propositions.

I'm going to pull the rest of the California Today article and check the SF Chronicle and McClatchy editorials, plus the Democratic and Republican party endorsements on Prop 5.
