Pros and Cons
Supporters of the recall process believe it provides a way for citizens to exercise control over elected officials who fail to represent their constituents' best interests, or who are unresponsive or incompetent. This view maintains that an elected representative is an agent or a servant of their constituents, not their master.
Opponents argue that recalls can lead to an excess of democracy: That the threat of a recall election lessens the independence of elected officials; undermines the principle of electing good officials and giving them a chance to govern; and can be abused by well-financed special interest groups and give them undue influence over the political process.
Process
How the Recall Process Works
The recall process varies in its details from one state to another, but in general, recall campaigns follow these steps:
File an application to circulate a recall petition (some states allow petitions only if they contain certain grounds for recall (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials#Grounds)).
Circulate a recall petition and gather a specified number of signatures in a specified period of time (view the detailed petitioning requirements (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials#Petition)).
Submit petitions to election officials for verification of signatures.
If enough valid signatures are presented, hold a recall election (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials#Election).
Grounds for Recall
In most of the recall states, any registered voter can begin a recall campaign for any reason. The language in Michigan's constitution is typical of most states: “The sufficiency of any statement of reasons or grounds ... shall be a political rather than a judicial question.” (Mich. Const. Art. II §8) Indeed, recall campaigns are often politically motivated. For example, in 2011, Republican senators in Wisconsin faced recalls for supporting the governor's effort to reduce the influence of public employee unions, and in Arizona, a senator faced recall for sponsoring a controversial immigration bill.
Specific grounds for recall are required in eight states:
Alaska: Lack of fitness, incompetence, neglect of duties or corruption (Alaska Stat. §15.45.510)
Georgia: Act of malfeasance or misconduct while in office; violation of oath of office; failure to perform duties prescribed by law; willfully misused, converted, or misappropriated, without authority, public property or public funds entrusted to or associated with the elective office to which the official has been elected or appointed. Discretionary performance of a lawful act or a prescribed duty shall not constitute a ground for recall of an elected public official. (Ga. Code §21-4-3(7) and 21-4-4(c))
Kansas: Conviction for a felony, misconduct in office or failure to perform duties prescribed by law. Misconduct in office means a violation of law by the officer that impacts the officer’s ability to perform the official duties of the office. No recall submitted to the voters shall be held void because of the insufficiency of the grounds, application, or petition by which the submission was procured. (Kan. Stat. Ann. §25-4302)
Minnesota: Serious malfeasance or nonfeasance during the term of office in the performance of the duties of the office or conviction during the term of office of a serious crime (Minn. Const. Art. VIII, §6).
Montana : Physical or mental lack of fitness, incompetence, violation of oath of office, official misconduct, conviction of certain felony offenses (enumerated in Title 45). No person may be recalled for performing a mandatory duty of the office he holds or for not performing any act that, if performed, would subject him to prosecution for official misconduct. (Mont. Code Ann. §2-16-603)
Rhode Island: Authorized in the case of a general officer who has been indicted or informed against for a felony, convicted of a misdemeanor or against whom a finding of probable cause of violation of the code of ethics has been made by the ethics commission. (R.I. Const. Art. IV, §1)
Virginia: Neglect of duty, misuse of office, or incompetence in the performance of duties when that neglect of duty, misuse of office, or incompetence in the performance of duties has a material adverse effect upon the conduct of the office, or upon conviction of a drug-related misdemeanor or a misdemeanor involving a "hate crime." (Va. Code Ann. §24.2-233)
Washington: Commission of some act or acts of malfeasance or misfeasance while in office, or who has violation of oath of office. (Wash. Const. Art. I §33)
In 2012, Michigan passed a law requiring that a recall petition must clearly and factually state the reason(s) for the recall, which must be based on the elected official's conduct during his or her term of office (Mich. Comp. Laws §168.951A). This differs from the specific grounds required in some other states, as Michigan’s requirement will not necessarily eliminate politically motivated recalls. For example, under this Michigan law a voter could initiate a recall against a legislator on the political grounds that the legislator voted against an issue the voter supports. As long as that allegation is stated clearly and factually, it would presumably meet this new criterion.
Circulating a Recall Petition
The recall process is similar to the ballot initiative process in that it requires the submission of citizen petitions. The number of signatures necessary to trigger a recall election, however, is often significantly higher than the number required for ballot initiatives. The required number of signatures is generally equal to a percentage of the vote in the last election for the office in question, although some states base the formula on the number of eligible voters or other numbers. These requirements are listed in the table below.
In many states that allow recalls, there are restrictions on when in an officer’s term a recall petition is permissible. For instance, in Kansas, “no application for the recall of a state officer may be filed during the first 120 days or last 200 days of the term” of the state officer. In Colorado and Michigan, recall petitions cannot be filed during the first or last six months of the term.

Nineteen states plus the District of Columbia permit the recall of state officials:

History
History and Use of the Recall in the U.S.
The recall device began in the United States in a municipality-Los Angeles-in 1903. Michigan and Oregon, in 1908, were the first states to adopt recall procedures for state officials. Illinois became the most recent state to adopt recall procedures for state officials when voters approved a constitutional amendment in 2010 to allow recall of the governor. Before that, Minnesota (1996) and New Jersey (1993) were the most recent.
Historically, recall attempts at the state level have been largely unsuccessful. The recall is used much more often, and with more success, at the local level.
Many attempts have been made to recall governors throughout U.S. history, but only four have gathered enough petition signatures to trigger recall elections. In 2021, California Gov. Gavin Newsom survived a recall election. In 2012, Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker survived a recall election. In 2003, California voters successfully recalled Gov. Gray Davis, and in North Dakota in 1921, voters successfully recalled not only Gov. Lynn J. Frazier, but also the attorney general and the commissioner of agriculture. In 1988, Arizona voters submitted enough signatures to trigger a recall election for Gov. Evan Mecham, but he was impeached by the state's House of Representatives before the scheduled recall election.
Recall efforts against state legislators are more common, but still unusual. Recall attempts against legislators have gathered enough signatures to trigger an election just 40 times. (Many more recall efforts are started and never make it to the election stage.) Eleven of those occurred in a single year, 2011. Forty-three percent of all legislative recall elections that have ever occurred were held between 2011 and 2013. However, only eight of those 17 elections succeeded in unseating a legislator. Overall, 53% of legislative recall elections have succeeded in unseating a legislator. Additionally, two legislators resigned after petitions with sufficient signatures to force recall elections against them were submitted.

The following is a list of every recall election of a state legislator throughout U.S. history. The fact that these elections occurred means that, in each of the following cases, enough signatures were gathered on petitions to trigger a recall election. Pros and Cons
Supporters of the recall process believe it provides a way for citizens to exercise control over elected officials who fail to represent their constituents' best interests, or who are unresponsive or incompetent. This view maintains that an elected representative is an agent or a servant of their constituents, not their master.
Opponents argue that recalls can lead to an excess of democracy: That the threat of a recall election lessens the independence of elected officials; undermines the principle of electing good officials and giving them a chance to govern; and can be abused by well-financed special interest groups and give them undue influence over the political process.
Process
How the Recall Process Works
The recall process varies in its details from one state to another, but in general, recall campaigns follow these steps:
File an application to circulate a recall petition (some states allow petitions only if they contain certain grounds for recall (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials#Grounds)).
Circulate a recall petition and gather a specified number of signatures in a specified period of time (view the detailed petitioning requirements (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials#Petition)).
Submit petitions to election officials for verification of signatures.
If enough valid signatures are presented, hold a recall election (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials#Election).
Grounds for Recall
In most of the recall states, any registered voter can begin a recall campaign for any reason. The language in Michigan's constitution is typical of most states: “The sufficiency of any statement of reasons or grounds ... shall be a political rather than a judicial question.” (Mich. Const. Art. II §8) Indeed, recall campaigns are often politically motivated. For example, in 2011, Republican senators in Wisconsin faced recalls for supporting the governor's effort to reduce the influence of public employee unions, and in Arizona, a senator faced recall for sponsoring a controversial immigration bill.
Specific grounds for recall are required in eight states:
Alaska: Lack of fitness, incompetence, neglect of duties or corruption (Alaska Stat. §15.45.510)
Georgia: Act of malfeasance or misconduct while in office; violation of oath of office; failure to perform duties prescribed by law; willfully misused, converted, or misappropriated, without authority, public property or public funds entrusted to or associated with the elective office to which the official has been elected or appointed. Discretionary performance of a lawful act or a prescribed duty shall not constitute a ground for recall of an elected public official. (Ga. Code §21-4-3(7) and 21-4-4(c))
Kansas: Conviction for a felony, misconduct in office or failure to perform duties prescribed by law. Misconduct in office means a violation of law by the officer that impacts the officer’s ability to perform the official duties of the office. No recall submitted to the voters shall be held void because of the insufficiency of the grounds, application, or petition by which the submission was procured. (Kan. Stat. Ann. §25-4302)
Minnesota: Serious malfeasance or nonfeasance during the term of office in the performance of the duties of the office or conviction during the term of office of a serious crime (Minn. Const. Art. VIII, §6).
Montana : Physical or mental lack of fitness, incompetence, violation of oath of office, official misconduct, conviction of certain felony offenses (enumerated in Title 45). No person may be recalled for performing a mandatory duty of the office he holds or for not performing any act that, if performed, would subject him to prosecution for official misconduct. (Mont. Code Ann. §2-16-603)
Rhode Island: Authorized in the case of a general officer who has been indicted or informed against for a felony, convicted of a misdemeanor or against whom a finding of probable cause of violation of the code of ethics has been made by the ethics commission. (R.I. Const. Art. IV, §1)
Virginia: Neglect of duty, misuse of office, or incompetence in the performance of duties when that neglect of duty, misuse of office, or incompetence in the performance of duties has a material adverse effect upon the conduct of the office, or upon conviction of a drug-related misdemeanor or a misdemeanor involving a "hate crime." (Va. Code Ann. §24.2-233)
Washington: Commission of some act or acts of malfeasance or misfeasance while in office, or who has violation of oath of office. (Wash. Const. Art. I §33)
In 2012, Michigan passed a law requiring that a recall petition must clearly and factually state the reason(s) for the recall, which must be based on the elected official's conduct during his or her term of office (Mich. Comp. Laws §168.951A). This differs from the specific grounds required in some other states, as Michigan’s requirement will not necessarily eliminate politically motivated recalls. For example, under this Michigan law a voter could initiate a recall against a legislator on the political grounds that the legislator voted against an issue the voter supports. As long as that allegation is stated clearly and factually, it would presumably meet this new criterion.
Circulating a Recall Petition
The recall process is similar to the ballot initiative process in that it requires the submission of citizen petitions. The number of signatures necessary to trigger a recall election, however, is often significantly higher than the number required for ballot initiatives. The required number of signatures is generally equal to a percentage of the vote in the last election for the office in question, although some states base the formula on the number of eligible voters or other numbers. In many states that allow recalls, there are restrictions on when in an officer’s term a recall petition is permissible. For instance, in Kansas, “no application for the recall of a state officer may be filed during the first 120 days or last 200 days of the term” of the state officer. In Colorado and Michigan, recall petitions cannot be filed during the first or last six months of the term.

I'm weighing whether the measure's partisan split should affect my own conclusion, so I'll ground my view in the reasoning and not in which party backs which side. The effects on appointments and succession would matter to whichever party is in power, so I'll keep that in mind as a point of fairness rather than a reason to pick a side.

I'm weighing whether the partisan split should count against the measure, since all the current statewide offices are held by Democrats and a Democratic governor would make the appointments after a recall. Under the status quo a recall replacement could go to either party, as Schwarzenegger's 2003 win showed, so the partisan effect is real and I'll treat it as a factor, not a settled verdict.

I'm noticing that the partisan effect cuts both ways: Prop 5 would tend to lock in whichever party holds the statewide offices after a recall, while the status quo lets a recall installed by an organized minority pick a replacement from either side. Both systems have partisan incidence, so this consideration is real but doesn't settle the question by itself.

I'm weighing the "No" side's strongest points: recalled officials could run again, legislative vacancies could sit empty for months, and the status quo has public legitimacy. I'm also noticing the partisan effect cuts both ways, and that the majority-rule argument may be less compelling to a skeptical reader than I'd assumed.

I'm checking the past recall results to see whether a minority winner really happened: Schwarzenegger in 2003 drew more votes than the "keep Davis" side, so that critique is weaker there. The 2018 state Senate case, with 50,000 votes against 66,000, is a clearer example of a minority winner, though it was a low-turnout special primary. The 2021 recall failed, so it produced no replacement at all.

I'm checking how the 2003 and 2018 replacements would have fared under Prop 5's majority test, which makes the minority-winner problem look rarer than the Yes side claims. The 2018 Senate case is the clearest example of a minority winner, and it's the one tied to the supermajority flip and the tax-vote concern.

I'm settling on how to frame the decision: a No vote could rest on the status quo's rare but real minority replacements being outweighed by Prop 5's gaps, appointments, and drafting problems, while a Yes vote could rest on aligning recall with normal majority rules. Both are defensible judgment calls, and the trade-offs don't clearly favor either side.

I'm weighing which way to land, since the majority-rule concern looks legitimate and the drafting problems look secondary, yet the eligibility and appointment trade-offs are real too. Whether that tilts toward Yes depends on how much weight a reader gives each side's values.

I'm weighing the harms each way: if I'm wrong about No, a governor could take office with only around 28–48% support, which seems a more serious legitimacy problem than a few months of legislative vacancy. That makes the worst case under the status quo look worse, so I'm leaning toward Yes.

I'm weighing the worst case under each choice: a governor with only around 28–48% support taking office looks more serious than a legislative seat sitting vacant for a few months. Prop 5's gaps are bounded, so I'm leaning toward Yes on the legitimacy grounds, while still weighing the voter-choice point that the status quo lets people pick the replacement directly.

I'm settling the cost question as roughly a wash, since legislative specials add expense while statewide recalls that replace a late-term governor save money. The majority-runoff requirement would add cost on top of that, but the overall picture is a measure whose design hangs together reasonably well, even if its trade-offs are real.

I'm also weighing how the partisan backing plays in: Newsom and the state Democratic Party support Prop 5 while Republicans oppose it, and the Senate vote lined up almost entirely along party lines. I'm not sure whether typical voters will weigh the majority-rule principle more heavily than the appeal of picking a replacement directly.

I'm checking the partisan backing and the Senate vote split, which seems to conflict with what I remembered about Republican opposition. I'll set that detail aside rather than chase it, and list the Yes and No considerations in plain terms to see which way they weigh.

Now I'm listing the remaining considerations as a tally: the interest-group incentive to install a replacement favors Yes, while losing the same-ballot choice, legislative vacancies, the appointment power over other statewide offices, the recalled official's eligibility to run again, and the title confusion all favor No. Costs look roughly neutral, and partisan entrenchment is the last item on the list.

I'm tallying the remaining considerations: partisan neutrality is a concern for some readers, public opinion is skeptical of the measure, and the status quo's long history counts for something. Reversibility seems ambiguous. The No side has more individual objections, while Yes rests mainly on the majority-rule principle, which carries real weight for me.

I'm going back and forth on whether the clause tips me toward Yes or No, since a recalled official could return to office after winning a majority in a special election. I'd call that odd rather than illegitimate, since voters would have effectively changed their minds, though the Chronicle treats it as a serious flaw.

I'm leaning toward No on the grounds that the measure bundles several design choices, like the recalled official's eligibility, months-long legislative vacancies, and gubernatorial appointments to other statewide offices, that the rare problem it targets doesn't clearly justify. Since recall events are uncommon, the stakes for an ordinary voter are small, so I'm weighing which principle matters more: majority rule, or not changing the constitution for a fix that introduces new problems.

content.text: Results aren't posted yet; the AP and KCRA pages show zero votes counted, so the election hasn't been decided. The most recent poll I've seen is mid-October. I'll confirm that poll directly and check the state-by-state data on how other states handle recall replacements.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-two percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 55 percent would vote no. Key Takeaways
Nineteen states allow recall of state officials, enabling citizens to remove elected officials before their terms end. Virginia has a process that is similar to recall, but involves a recall trial, where a circuit court determines whether to remove an elected official, rather than an election.
Recall processes vary across states, but generally a recall effort involves collecting a certain number of signatures on a petition within a set timeframe. After a petition meeting the requirements is submitted to the appropriate authority and verified, a recall election is held.
NOTE: The following is presented for informational purposes only. NCSL does not provide advice on how to conduct a recall campaign in any state. For the specific procedures to be followed in any state, please contact your state's election official s (https://www.eac.gov/voters/register-and-vote-in-your-state) .
Introduction
In the 19 states that allow state recall elections, citizens can attempt to remove an elected official from office. Typically, the recall process consists of gathering a certain number of signatures on a petition in a certain amount of time. Beyond this, details of the recall process vary by state. This page explains these processes and provides a list of each state's laws governing the recall of state officials.
Overview
Recall is a procedure that allows citizens to remove and replace a public official before the official’s term of office ends. Historically, recall has been used most frequently at the local level. By some estimates, three-fourths of recall elections are at the city council or school board level. This webpage, however, focuses on the recall only as it applies to state officials.
Recall differs from another method for removing officials from office—impeachment (https://www.ncsl.org/about-state-legislatures/separation-of-powers-impeachment)—in that it is a political device while impeachment is a legal process. Impeachment typically requires a state legislature’s lower chamber to bring specific charges, and the upper chamber to act as the jury in an impeachment trial. In contrast, in most of the 19 recall states specific grounds for recall are not required, and the recall of a state official is accomplished through an election.
Nineteen states plus the District of Columbia permit the recall of state officials:
Alaska – Const. Art. 11, §8; Alaska Stat. §15.45.470-15.45.710
Arizona – Const. Art. 8, Pt. 1, §1-6; Ariz. Rev. Stat.
California – Const. Art 2, §13-19; Cal. Elec. Code §11000-11386
Colorado – Const. Art. 21, Colo. Rev. Stat. §1-12-101 – 1-12-123
District of Columbia – D.C. Code §1-1001.17, §1-204.111 et seq.
Georgia – Const. Art. §2, Para. 4; Ga. Code §21-4-1 et seq.
Idaho – Const. Art. 6, §6; Idaho Code §34-1701 – 34-1715
Illinois – Const. Art. 3, §7
Kansas – Const. Art, 4, §3; Kan. Stat. Ann. §25-4301 – 25-4331
Louisiana – Const. Art. 10, §26; La. Stat. Ann. §18:1300.1 - 18:1300.17
Michigan – Const. Art. 2, §8; Mich. Comp. Laws §168.951 - 168.977
Minnesota – Const. Art. 8, §6; Minn. Stat. Ann. §211C.01 et seq.
Montana – Mont. Code Ann. §2-16-601 – 2-16-635
Nevada – Const. Art. 2, §9; Nev. Rev. Stat. §294A.006, §306.005 et seq.
New Jersey – Const. Art. 1, §2(b); N.J. Rev. Stat. Ann. §19:27A-1 – 19:27A-18
North Dakota – Const. Art. 3, §1 and §10; N.D. Cent. Code §16.1-01-09.1
Oregon – Const. Art. 2, §18; Or. Rev. Stat. §249.865 - 249.877
Rhode Island – Const. Art. 4, §1
Washington – Const. Art. 1, Sec. 33-34; Wash Rev. Code §29A.56.110 - 29A.56.270
Wisconsin – Const. Art. 13, §12; Wis. Stat. Ann. §9.10
All these states lay out the right to recall elected officials in their constitutions, with the exception of Montana, where the right to recall is found only in state statutes. Additionally, each recall state except Illinois and Rhode Island further explains its recall processes in state statutes.
Virginia (https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacodefull/title24.2/chapter2/article7/) has a process that is similar to recall, but it is not listed here as a recall state because its process, while requiring citizen petitions, calls for a recall trial rather than an election (Va. Code Ann. §24.2-233 – 24.2.238). In Virginia, after a petition containing the required number of signatures is verified, a circuit court decides whether a Virginia official will be removed from office. In the recall states, the voters decide in an election. Currently, only these 19 states allow recall elections of statewide elected officials, but other states have considered establishing recall procedures. For state legislative action on recalls and other election topics, reference NCSL’s state elections legislation database (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/state-election-legislation-database) and the archived database (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/state-elections-legislation-archived-database), which has legislation from 2011 to 2024.
Read More
History
History and Use of the Recall in the U.S.
The recall device began in the United States in a municipality-Los Angeles-in 1903. Michigan and Oregon, in 1908, were the first states to adopt recall procedures for state officials. Illinois became the most recent state to adopt recall procedures for state officials when voters approved a constitutional amendment in 2010 to allow recall of the governor. Before that, Minnesota (1996) and New Jersey (1993) were the most recent.
Historically, recall attempts at the state level have been largely unsuccessful. The recall is used much more often, and with more success, at the local level.
Many attempts have been made to recall governors throughout U.S. history, but only four have gathered enough petition signatures to trigger recall elections. In 2021, California Gov. Gavin Newsom survived a recall election. In 2012, Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker survived a recall election. In 2003, California voters successfully recalled Gov. Gray Davis, and in North Dakota in 1921, voters successfully recalled not only Gov. Lynn J. Frazier, but also the attorney general and the commissioner of agriculture. In 1988, Arizona voters submitted enough signatures to trigger a recall election for Gov. Evan Mecham, but he was impeached by the state's House of Representatives before the scheduled recall election.
Recall efforts against state legislators are more common, but still unusual. Recall attempts against legislators have gathered enough signatures to trigger an election just 40 times. (Many more recall efforts are started and never make it to the election stage.) Eleven of those occurred in a single year, 2011. Forty-three percent of all legislative recall elections that have ever occurred were held between 2011 and 2013. However, only eight of those 17 elections succeeded in unseating a legislator. Overall, 53% of legislative recall elections have succeeded in unseating a legislator. Additionally, two legislators resigned after petitions with sufficient signatures to force recall elections against them were submitted.
All Recall Elections Held in the U.S. for State Legislators
The following is a list of every recall election of a state legislator throughout U.S. history. The fact that these elections occurred means that, in each of the following cases, enough signatures were gathered on petitions to trigger a recall election. Officials on this list who "survived recall election" are people who were not voted out of office in the subsequent recall election. Officials who were "successfully recalled" on this list are people who were voted out of office in that election.

Read More
Pros and Cons
Supporters of the recall process believe it provides a way for citizens to exercise control over elected officials who fail to represent their constituents' best interests, or who are unresponsive or incompetent. This view maintains that an elected representative is an agent or a servant of their constituents, not their master.
Opponents argue that recalls can lead to an excess of democracy: That the threat of a recall election lessens the independence of elected officials; undermines the principle of electing good officials and giving them a chance to govern; and can be abused by well-financed special interest groups and give them undue influence over the political process.
Process
How the Recall Process Works
The recall process varies in its details from one state to another, but in general, recall campaigns follow these steps:
File an application to circulate a recall petition (some states allow petitions only if they contain certain grounds for recall (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials#Grounds)).
Circulate a recall petition and gather a specified number of signatures in a specified period of time (view the detailed petitioning requirements (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials#Petition)).
Submit petitions to election officials for verification of signatures.
If enough valid signatures are presented, hold a recall election (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials#Election).
Grounds for Recall
In most of the recall states, any registered voter can begin a recall campaign for any reason. The language in Michigan's constitution is typical of most states: “The sufficiency of any statement of reasons or grounds ... shall be a political rather than a judicial question.” (Mich. Const. Art. II §8) Indeed, recall campaigns are often politically motivated. For example, in 2011, Republican senators in Wisconsin faced recalls for supporting the governor's effort to reduce the influence of public employee unions, and in Arizona, a senator faced recall for sponsoring a controversial immigration bill.
Specific grounds for recall are required in eight states:
Alaska: Lack of fitness, incompetence, neglect of duties or corruption (Alaska Stat. §15.45.510)
Georgia: Act of malfeasance or misconduct while in office; violation of oath of office; failure to perform duties prescribed by law; willfully misused, converted, or misappropriated, without authority, public property or public funds entrusted to or associated with the elective office to which the official has been elected or appointed. Discretionary performance of a lawful act or a prescribed duty shall not constitute a ground for recall of an elected public official. (Ga. Code §21-4-3(7) and 21-4-4(c))
Kansas: Conviction for a felony, misconduct in office or failure to perform duties prescribed by law. Misconduct in office means a violation of law by the officer that impacts the officer’s ability to perform the official duties of the office. No recall submitted to the voters shall be held void because of the insufficiency of the grounds, application, or petition by which the submission was procured. (Kan. Stat. Ann. §25-4302)
Minnesota: Serious malfeasance or nonfeasance during the term of office in the performance of the duties of the office or conviction during the term of office of a serious crime (Minn. Const. Art. VIII, §6).
Montana : Physical or mental lack of fitness, incompetence, violation of oath of office, official misconduct, conviction of certain felony offenses (enumerated in Title 45). No person may be recalled for performing a mandatory duty of the office he holds or for not performing any act that, if performed, would subject him to prosecution for official misconduct. (Mont. Code Ann. §2-16-603)
Rhode Island: Authorized in the case of a general officer who has been indicted or informed against for a felony, convicted of a misdemeanor or against whom a finding of probable cause of violation of the code of ethics has been made by the ethics commission. (R.I. Const. Art. IV, §1)
Virginia: Neglect of duty, misuse of office, or incompetence in the performance of duties when that neglect of duty, misuse of office, or incompetence in the performance of duties has a material adverse effect upon the conduct of the office, or upon conviction of a drug-related misdemeanor or a misdemeanor involving a "hate crime." (Va. Code Ann. §24.2-233)
Washington: Commission of some act or acts of malfeasance or misfeasance while in office, or who has violation of oath of office. (Wash. Const. Art. I §33)
In 2012, Michigan passed a law requiring that a recall petition must clearly and factually state the reason(s) for the recall, which must be based on the elected official's conduct during his or her term of office (Mich. Comp. Laws §168.951A). This differs from the specific grounds required in some other states, as Michigan’s requirement will not necessarily eliminate politically motivated recalls. For example, under this Michigan law a voter could initiate a recall against a legislator on the political grounds that the legislator voted against an issue the voter supports. As long as that allegation is stated clearly and factually, it would presumably meet this new criterion.
Circulating a Recall Petition
The recall process is similar to the ballot initiative process in that it requires the submission of citizen petitions. The number of signatures necessary to trigger a recall election, however, is often significantly higher than the number required for ballot initiatives. The required number of signatures is generally equal to a percentage of the vote in the last election for the office in question, although some states base the formula on the number of eligible voters or other numbers. In many states that allow recalls, there are restrictions on when in an officer’s term a recall petition is permissible. For instance, in Kansas, “no application for the recall of a state officer may be filed during the first 120 days or last 200 days of the term” of the state officer. In Colorado and Michigan, recall petitions cannot be filed during the first or last six months of the term.

Proposition 5 rewrites three sections of the California Constitution
The text of proposed law (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) amends Article II, sections 15 and 17, and Article V, section 10. It changes no statute directly. Its edits are short:
Section 15(a) strikes the words "and, if appropriate, to elect a successor" from the description of a recall election, leaving an election "to determine whether to recall an officer."
Section 15(c) strikes the sentence that makes "the candidate who receives a plurality" the successor, and strikes the ban on the targeted officer being a candidate. In their place it provides that if the majority votes to recall, "the officer is removed and the office shall be vacant. The vacancy shall be filled in accordance with this Constitution and statute, provided that the officer who was the subject of the recall election shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office."
Article V, section 10(b) is new. If the Governor is removed by recall, "the Lieutenant Governor shall become Governor for the remainder of the unexpired term," unless the recall comes "before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the Governor's term." In that case "a special election shall be called to replace the Governor," consolidated with the statewide primary; a candidate with a majority at the primary takes office, and otherwise "the top two vote-getters shall compete in a special election consolidated with the subsequent statewide general election."
Section 17 moves the job of running a governor's recall from the lieutenant governor, who would now be the successor, to the secretary of state, with the controller taking over if the governor and secretary of state are targeted at the same time.
The Attorney General's ballot label calls it a change for "statewide officers," but the text applies to every state officer subject to recall, and the LAO's analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm) describes its effect on Senate and Assembly seats as well. Prop 5 does not change how a recall qualifies, how quickly the election is held, or how local recalls work.
California recall law today: 12% of the last vote, two questions, a plurality winner
The power to recall is in Article II (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2014.&article=II) of the Constitution: "Recall is the power of the electors to remove an elective officer." A recall of a statewide officer needs signatures equal to 12% of the last vote for the office, including 1% of the last vote in each of five counties; senators, Assembly members, Board of Equalization members and appellate and trial judges need 20%. Proponents have 160 days to gather them, and the "sufficiency of reason is not reviewable." Once signatures are certified, the election is held 60 to 80 days later, or within 180 days to coincide with a regular election. An officer who survives is reimbursed for recall expenses, and no new recall can begin for six months.
The successor rule sits in section 15(c), last amended by Proposition 183 in 1994: if the majority votes to recall, "the officer is removed and, if there is a candidate, the candidate who receives a plurality is the successor. The officer may not be a candidate." Elections Code section 11385 repeats it: the candidate "receiving the highest number of votes for the office shall be declared elected for the unexpired term."
Prop 5 would replace that with the rules California already uses when an office falls vacant for any other reason. The lieutenant governor becomes governor under Article V, section 10 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=V). For the lieutenant governor, secretary of state, controller, treasurer, attorney general, superintendent of public instruction and Board of Equalization, Article V, section 5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%205.&article=V) has the governor nominate a replacement who takes office on confirmation by a majority of each house, or automatically if neither house acts within 90 days. For a legislative seat, Elections Code section 10703 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=10703) requires a special election "at least 126 days, but not more than 140 days" after the governor's proclamation, which must be issued within 14 days of the vacancy.
California has already made this change for local officials. Since January 1, 2023, under AB 2582 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB2582), recalls of local officers have asked only whether to remove the officer; under Elections Code section 11382 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=11382) the office "shall be vacant until it is filled according to law," and the recalled officer may not be appointed to the vacancy. Prop 5 uses the same structure and much of the same wording for state offices, which only a constitutional amendment can reach.
California recall elections are keeping their signature thresholds and timelines under Proposition 5 while the replacement question gives way to succession, appointment and special elections, as the measure's text and the California Constitution show in October 2026. The governor's seat under Prop 5: The lieutenant governor, then possibly a special election
For a recalled governor, Prop 5 creates a two-track rule keyed to timing. Late in a term, the lieutenant governor serves out the remainder, and no election is held for the seat until the next regular gubernatorial election. Early in a term, before the nomination period closes for the next statewide election during the governor's first two years, the lieutenant governor takes over and a special election is held alongside the next statewide primary. A majority winner there serves the rest of the term; without one, the top two meet again on the November ballot. The LAO's summary: the lieutenant governor "serves as Governor until voters elect a new Governor at a future statewide election" in the first case and "for the rest of the term" in the second.
Because Prop 5 removes the constitutional bar on the recalled officer's candidacy, a governor recalled early in a term could appear in that special election. The same applies to a recalled legislator in the special election that would fill the seat. The only limit the text adds is on appointment: a recalled officer "shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office."
That provision is the one even the measure's author has not defended. Newman told the San Francisco Chronicle's editorial board he could not explain why it is there: "I'm honestly not sure," he said (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-5-recall-california-22458510.php). "It wouldn't pain me if it wasn't there." The Yes campaign's website (https://fixtherecall.com/) presents it as a feature, saying that today's process "locks the recalled official out of the race entirely" and that under Prop 5 "the seat goes to a special election where every candidate can run." That description fits legislative seats and an early-term governor recall; for a governor recalled late in a term and for other statewide offices, the text provides succession or appointment, not an election.
California recall history: 182 attempts, 11 elections, six removals since 1913
The Secretary of State counts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) 182 attempts to recall state officials since 1913, 57 of them against governors. Eleven qualified for the ballot: nine against legislators and two against governors. Six succeeded: Senators Marshall Black (1913) and Edwin Grant (1914), Assembly members Paul Horcher (1994) and Doris Allen (1995), Governor Gray Davis (2003) and Senator Josh Newman (2018). No state recall effort is in circulation now, according to the Secretary of State's current-efforts page (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/current-recall-efforts).
The three most recent recalls show what the replacement question does. In 2003 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2003-special/sum.pdf), 55.4% voted to recall Davis, and Arnold Schwarzenegger won the replacement contest with 4,206,284 votes, 48.6% of the votes for a candidate and more than the 4,007,783 cast to keep Davis. In 2018 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2018-primary/sov/15-state-senator-29th-district.pdf), 58.1% voted to recall Newman in the 29th Senate District, and Republican Ling Ling Chang won the seat with 50,215 votes, 33.8% of the replacement vote and 15,982 fewer than the 66,197 cast for Newman to stay. In 2021 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/11-sov-summary.pdf), 61.9% voted against recalling Governor Newsom; the leading replacement candidate, Larry Elder, received 3,563,867 votes, which would have made him governor with 27.8% of the votes cast on the recall question had the recall passed. That is the "about 28%" figure in the Yes argument.
California recall results are showing replacement winners at 46.8% and 31.8% of the recall vote in 2003 and 2018, and 27.8% for 2021's leading candidate, in Secretary of State data compiled in October 2026. California is one of seven states that choose a successor on the same ballot as the recall, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures' survey (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials) of the 19 states that allow recall of state officials. Five others hold a separate special election and eight fill the vacancy by appointment, with some states mixing methods by office. Other reform ideas have taken different routes: the state's Little Hoover Commission recommended (https://lhc.ca.gov/press-release-43/) in 2022 a "snap" election in which "the targeted official is placed on the ballot with all potential replacements," plus a statewide signature threshold of 10% of registered voters. Prop 5 adopts neither.
Prop 5's cost: Savings or costs "in the range of millions of dollars," depending on the recall
The LAO's fiscal estimate (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm) is "unknown," because it depends on how often recalls happen and which offices they target. Removing the second question would save money on ballots and voter materials when no follow-up election is needed, which is the case for a governor recalled late in a term and for offices filled by appointment. A legislative recall would cost more if the follow-up special election "could not be consolidated with a scheduled election," at "millions of dollars per election." The LAO puts the net effect at "savings or costs potentially in the range of millions of dollars," less than 0.1% of the General Fund.
For scale, the Department of Finance's July 1, 2021 letter (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2021-recall/dof-allocation-costs-letter.pdf) estimated $243.6 million for counties and $32.4 million for the Secretary of State, $276 million in all, of which the Legislature appropriated $250.2 million; the same letter estimated $90.6 million if the recall had been consolidated with a regular election. Prop 5 does not change the cost of the recall election itself, only of what follows it.
Proposition 5's author and the vote in the Legislature
Newman, a Fullerton Democrat, introduced SCA 1 in January 2023. It passed the Senate 31–7 on February 1, 2024 and, after amendment, the Assembly 59–17 on August 30, 2024; the Senate concurred 32–8 the next day, and it was filed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) with the Secretary of State on September 10, 2024, directed to this November's ballot. Constitutional amendments need two-thirds of each house. The Chronicle's editorial board notes that Newman was recalled in 2018, won the seat back in 2020 and lost again in 2024. Of the 2018 recall, which his opponents tie to his vote to raise gas taxes, he told CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-proposition-5-explainer/): "I didn't do anything other than cast a tough vote."
Nobody is spending money on the measure. The Secretary of State's contribution page (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-5-sca-1-newman-elections-recall-state-officers-res-ch-204-2024) for Prop 5 reports "No committees identified" on either side as of October 6, and no Prop 5 committee appears on the FPPC's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), which covers committees that have raised $1 million. The Yes campaign's website is paid for by Californians For a Prosperous Golden State, the committee listed with Newman as the ballot contact. No opposition contact is listed in the Voter Information Guide.
The arguments: Majority rule versus the voters' pick
The Yes argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by the League of Women Voters of California, California Common Cause and former FPPC chair Dan Schnur, says the two questions together create "a dangerous loophole": "An elected official can be removed by a narrow majority. Then, a candidate listed in question #2 can win the office with far less than 50% of the votes cast." It cites the 2021 recall's cost as "more than $200 million" and says Prop 5 would stop recalls being used "to 'redo' an election as a political or partisan scheme." The Department of Finance's figures above support the cost claim; the 28% figure matches the Statement of Vote.
The No argument, signed by Senate Minority Leader Brian Jones and Assemblymember Joe Patterson, says Prop 5 "will take away your voice" because "politicians themselves—not voters—would choose who fills the vacancy" in many cases, and other seats "would sit vacant until another costly election." It objects that "that failed politician you just ran out the door… they'd be allowed to run in that next election," and its rebuttal says the author wants to change the rules after being recalled "when he raised taxes after breaking campaign promises." Carl DeMaio, the Prop 39 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/yes-voter-id-laws-are-on-the-california-ballot-proposition-39s-rules-costs-and-court-fights/) proponent, told CalMatters voters could be "without a representative for months, if not longer." Polling and endorsements on Proposition 5
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters, reading the ballot title "Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers," found 35% yes, 59% no and 5% undecided, the weakest position of any measure on the ballot. Opposition crossed party lines: Democrats 40% yes to 54% no, Republicans 34% to 64%, independents 28% to 65%. Asked which of the 14 measures interested them most, 1% named Prop 5. No other independent poll has published a Prop 5 result.
The parties split along legislative lines: the California Democratic Party supports (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) Prop 5 and the California Republican Party opposes (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) it. Governor Newsom, the target of the 2021 recall, plans to vote yes, according to the San Francisco Chronicle's account (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of the positions his campaign released on October 9. The editorial boards are divided. McClatchy's California board, writing for the Sacramento Bee and four other papers, endorsed (https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/proposition-5-could-change-california-173000601.html) it on September 18 because it "respects the democratic norm of majority rule." The San Francisco Chronicle's board recommended a no vote on October 8: it agreed "the second question is problematic" but called the provision letting recalled officials run again "a completely unnecessary provision" and "reason enough for voters to reject this measure."
Proposition 5 after November 3: A one-question recall from mid-December or the 1994 rule
If Prop 5 passes, it takes effect under Article XVIII, section 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII) on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote, which is due December 11. Any state recall after that would ask a single question, and the Elections Code sections that still describe a successor contest, such as section 11385, would sit under an amended Constitution that no longer provides for one. If it fails, state recalls keep the two-question ballot and plurality winner that section 15 has required since 1994, while local recalls continue under the one-question rule in place since 2023. Either way, the signature thresholds that decide how often Californians face a recall are not on this ballot.
This article reflects the Voter Information Guide as published, Secretary of State and FPPC campaign-finance data as of October 6, 2026, endorsements as of October 12, 2026, and polling fielded through September 10, 2026.

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.
Endorsement guide: S.F. Chronicle Endorsements for the 2026 California Election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Also: Y (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)es or no? Here are the Chronicle’s endorsements for California Supreme Court and appeals courts (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)
Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

But it is there. And the inability or unwillingness of lawmakers to put forth a simple, clean reform effort is reason enough for voters to reject this measure.
California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

Proposition 5 could change California’s recall elections. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Fri, September 18, 2026 at 5:30 PM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.
A volunteer with the Recall Gavin Newsom campaign collects signatures in Rancho Cordova on Jan. 23, 2021. On the election ballot this November, Proposition 5 will ask voters to consider changing how recall elections are held in California.
Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html) seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide. Such elections have been rare in California.
According to theLegislative Analyst's Office, (https://lao.ca.gov/) only 11 state recall efforts targeting nine legislators and two governors have qualified for the ballot since 1913. In 2003, Gray Davis (https://www.modbee.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/article251385288.html) became the only California governor to be recalled, a fate that also befell five state legislators over the years. The last statewide recall effort to qualify for the ballot was the unsuccessful campaign to oust Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/editorials/article253266413.html)
Under current law, voters are asked two questions in the same election when a recall effort qualifies for the ballot. The first is whether a state officer should be recalled. The second is who should replace that officer from a field of hopefuls seeking consideration if a recall is successful. In 2003, 135 candidates wanted to succeed Davis. In 2021, there were 46 candidates vying for Newsom's job.
THE BEE'S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html)
If Prop. 5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled. If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held. If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor. Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until a special election was held. If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that's more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It's why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop. 5.
Recall elections in California
Since California voters approved the recall process in 1911, five replacement candidates have been elected after six officials were removed from office with less than 50% of the vote. In California recall elections, the candidate who receives the most votes wins, unlike in a special election, where a candidate must win a majority.
Advertisement
Advertisement
This creates a conundrum of a recalled official garnering more voter support than the replacement candidate who "wins" the recall.
In the 2018 recall of former stateSen. Josh Newman, for instance, (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article145349124.html) his replacement, Republican Ling Ling Chang, came out on top with just under 34% of the vote. Newman points out that he had more votes in his favor; nearly 42% of voters opposed his recall.
"So I got more votes by way of 'no, don't kick him out,' than she got by 'yes, please put her in,'" Newman said.
Newman won back his Senate seat in the next regular election and then went on to write Prop. 5 (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-voters-prop-5-changes-recall-election-process/73175034).
One of the proposition's most outspoken opponents is Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a former talk radio host who pushed for Newman's recall in 2017.
How Prop. 5 opponents feel
DeMaio sees Prop. 5 as an attempt by the ruling party to evade recalls. "What they want to do is create a situation where politicians trying to fend off a recall can say, 'Don't vote for the recall or else you won't be represented for 12 months. You'll lose your voice,'" he told us.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Actually, Article II, Section 15 of the California Constitution, says a recall election must be held within 60 and 80 days of recall petition signatures being certified. The election may be held within 180 days of certification if it is consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election.
Arguments against Prop. 5 ignore that the current system created instances where replacement candidates got elected with less than 50% of the vote.
They decry the cost of conducting special elections and oppose that Prop. 5 would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the vacancy.
There have been 182 attempts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) to recall state officials in California. Eleven of those made the ballot, and only six were successful.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Some view the current recall system as "a weapon for political operators (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5.pdf) to undo election results they don't like," to quote the League of Women Voters and others.
Prop. 5 cannot put an end to the political gamesmanship, but it can safeguard the will of the voters by following the principle of majority rule.
McClatchy Media's California editorial board strongly urges a "yes" vote on Proposition 5.
