Here’s how Newsom is voting on California’s propositions
By Sophia Bollag (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/sophia-bollag/) , Staff Writer Oct 9, 2026
California Gov. Gavin Newsom pauses while discussing environmental issues in San Francisco on Sept. 29, 2026.
Rich Pedroncelli/Associated Press
SACRAMENTO — Gavin Newsom’s campaign team on Friday released an almost complete list of the governor’s positions on the ballot measures California voters will decide (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-ballot-measures-propositions-22507044.php) in the Nov. 3 midterm election.
Opinion: This is the worst measure on California’s ballot — and Gavin Newsom supports it (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/emilyhoeven/article/prop-38-california-newsom-22495203.php)
Chronicle endorsements: Editorial board’s recommendations for 2026 election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Newsom says he will vote no on four measures:
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Proposition 43: a measure that would make it harder for local governments to pass new taxes by raising the approval threshold for some new local taxes from majority to two-thirds
Proposition 44: a measure to require nonprofit federally qualified health centers to spend at least 90% of their revenue on program services that advance their charitable mission
Proposition 39: Newsom previously announced his opposition to this measure, which would impose new voter ID requirements for Californians
Proposition 40: Newsom has already appeared in ads against this measure, which would impose a new wealth tax on billionaire residents
He plans to vote for eight measures:
Proposition 1: a measure to let California borrow $11.25 billion for housing, with $10 billion for affordable rental housing and homeownership programs and $1.25 billion for veteran farm, home and mobile home purchase assistance
Proposition 2: a constitutional amendment to increase the amount of money California saves in budget reserves
Proposition 3: a measure to make permanent California’s existing higher income tax rates on high earners, which are otherwise scheduled to expire after 2030
Proposition 4: a measure that would allow state and local governments to create public financing programs for candidates who meet eligibility rules and spending limits, while barring use of those funds for legal defense fees, fines or personal campaign loans
Proposition 5: a measure inspired in part by the effort to recall Newsom in 2021 that would make statewide recalls in California simple yes or no contests for or against the removal of a politician and end the practice of voters also choosing a successor in the same election
Proposition 37: a measure to authorize up to $25 billion in bonds to fund loans for middle-income buyers of new homes
Proposition 38: a measure to authorize $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, split between a University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for public or nonprofit research institutions
Proposition 42: one of two measures designed to invalidate Proposition 40, the billionaire tax, this constitutional amendment would prohibit new state taxes on the ownership or control of personal property
Newsom is still reviewing Propositions 41 and 45, spokesperson Izzy Gardon said, and has not yet taken a position on them. Proposition 41 is the second measure designed to invalidate the billionaire tax if it passes and would require audits for programs funded by new statewide special taxes and prohibit new state taxes that would circumvent the state spending limit. Proposition 45 would limit environmental review under the California Environmental Quality Act for many new construction projects.

I'm weighing Prop 5's separate replacement process against the status quo's plurality rule, and noting that the Yes side's strongest point is the majority requirement. A recalled official could run again in the special election and win if they earn majority support, though the SF Chronicle calls that provision unnecessary and even Newman seems unsure why it's there. I still need to verify the Article V, section 5 language on whether gubernatorial appointments of statewide officers require Senate confirmation, since that bears on the claim about politicians choosing replacements.

California Must Address Weakness in the State’s Recall System, Urges Little Hoover Commission
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
February 8, 2022
For Additional Information Contact:
Ethan Rarick, Executive Director (510) 205-8042
California should adjust the signature requirement for recalling statewide office-holders and revise the recall election process to put the incumbent on the ballot against all challengers, urges the state’s independent government watchdog in its new report.
In Reforming the Recall (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall) the Little Hoover Commission evaluates the state’s recall process, examines the advantages and drawbacks of different recall reforms, and offers recommendations to strengthen the recall system.
“The recall is a popular tool of direct democracy that has been a significant component of the state’s electoral system for over a century,” says Commission Chair Pedro Nava. “We must keep the recall, but California must address fundamental flaws within current recall procedures that leave the system vulnerable to abuse and pave the way for a potentially undemocratic outcome.”
In its report, the Commission recommends that California change the signature requirement for recalling statewide office-holders from 12 percent of the vote in the last election for the office to 10 percent of registered voters. This adjustment will reduce fluctuations in the signature threshold as a result of differences in voter turnout between elections, providing greater consistency in the recall process. It will also increase the number of signatures required to initiate a recall election, discouraging overuse of the recall while keeping it accessible as a tool of electoral accountability.
The Commission further recommends that the state replace the existing two-part recall ballot with a “snap” special recall election. Under this system, the targeted official is placed on the ballot with all potential replacements.
“Under the current recall system a replacement candidate can win office even if they received fewer votes than the recalled incumbent,” says Chair Nava. “The core reason that the Commission supports the use of snap elections for recalls is that it would protect the democratic principle that the person who receives the most votes should win.”
The report follows a lengthy study process that included three public hearings at which Commissioners heard testimony from current and former elected officials such as Secretary of State Shirley Weber and former Secretary of State Bill Jones. The Commission also took testimony from a wide array of scholars and other experts, and received comment from more than 150 members of the public.
The Commission also outlines procedural reforms, which would give elections officials more time to administer elections and provide greater clarity around the recall process.
Several of the Commission’s recommendations—including those outlined above—must be approved by voters. The Commission urges the Legislature to propose recall reforms separately, to give voters the opportunity to pick which changes they think should be adopted.
“The Commission’s recommendations will bolster California’s recall system by helping the state better balance voters’ right to recall officials with protection for electoral integrity and democratic principles,” says Chair Nava.
About the Little Hoover Commission
The Little Hoover Commission is America’s only permanent, independent citizens commission working to improve state government. A nonpartisan oversight agency created in 1962, the Commission includes 13 Commissioners appointed by the Governor and legislative leaders. The Commission’s mission is to investigate state operations and promote efficiency, economy, and improved service.

SEC. 5.
(a) Unless the law otherwise provides, the Governor may fill a vacancy in office by appointment until a successor qualifies.
(b) Whenever there is a vacancy in the office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction, the Lieutenant Governor, Secretary of State, Controller, Treasurer, or Attorney General, or on the State Board of Equalization, the Governor shall nominate a person to fill the vacancy who shall take office upon confirmation by a majority of the membership of the Senate and a majority of the membership of
the Assembly and who shall hold office for the balance of the unexpired term. In the event the nominee is neither confirmed nor refused confirmation by both the Senate and the Assembly within 90 days of the submission of the nomination, the nominee shall take office as if he or she had been confirmed by a majority of the Senate and Assembly; provided, that if such 90-day period ends during a recess of the Legislature, the period shall be extended until the sixth day following the day on which the Legislature reconvenes.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 4:32 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:07 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What problem would Prop. 5 create?
A disincentive for the people to self-govern, leading to more distrust of government and restlessness of the “masses.” After a time of withdrawal and lack of participation, the people will feel and react to their oppression in a negative way. Oppressed people eventually revolt, and it’s never pretty.

We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
Currently, the recall process allows a candidate to win office without a majority. Why is that a system not worth reforming?
Under the current system, the democratic process of self-governance is served, and infinite amounts of taxpayer funds are saved by the current one-step process.
Prop. 5 “reforms” the current process by taking power from the people, and — worse — punishing the people for having the audacity to self-govern.
In the case of a recall, the term of office is limited to the remainder of the term of the recalled individual, and awarding the win to the person receiving a plurality in a crowded field is much more protective of the “democratic process” than adopting the changes proposed by Prop. 5, where the Sacramento insiders are the winners, hundreds of millions of dollars are wasted, and democracy dies.
If this measure isn’t a solution for fixing the recall process, do you have an alternate proposal?
This question pre-supposes the recall process needs fixing. The current process, wherein a recall decision and a filling of the recalled position in the case of recall success on the same ballot is efficient, fiscally responsible and respectful to the public.
The suggestion that the cost of having part two of the recall ballot is negligible, let alone millions of dollars, is patently absurd. Also absurd is the Prop. 5 proposal to eventually fill the recalled position with another, delayed election. The cost of a second election, which is likely to lead to a runoff costing more millions, is unarguable. That’s the very definition of absurd.
To quote Sen. Jones, “Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he (voted to raise) taxes after breaking campaign promises.”
What’s the biggest misconception about Prop. 5?
That there’s something wrong with the current system, and that CA legislators have any respect for a government of, by and for the people. CA is no longer a republic, but a socialist oligarchy. The power of the people to govern themselves has been so diminished already as to be virtually eliminated, and Prop. 5 is another step to seal the deal for complete power of the elite.
What did we miss? What didn’t we ask that our readers should know?
The element of Prop. 5 dealing with gubernatorial succession is also faulty. Yes, the people ostensibly elected a lieutenant governor, to serve as governor in the event of incapacity or death of the elected governor, not in the event of the governor’s disgrace — by which the lieutenant governor is surely tainted.
If the lieutenant governor wishes to succeed the governor in the event of a recall, that person may appear on the second portion of the ballot.
Chances are virtually 100% that if the people have grown disenchanted with the governor’s performance, they will be equally unwilling to be represented in that office by the second in command — almost certainly complicit in every act of disappointment and betrayal by the governor.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: October 20, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 21, 2026 at 11:17 AM PDT

When California Governor Gray Davis was the subject of a recall effort in 2003, he said in a televised speech (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.htmlhttps:/www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.html) at UCLA that he thought the recall would damage “the very fabric of our democracy.”
Elected officials may not like to see accountability arrive earlier than expected, but that doesn’t make Californians’ recall powers a threat to democracy.
While Proposition 5 doesn’t attack the people’s ability to hold a recall election, it does tinker with how a replacement candidate is selected.
Related Articles
Endorsement: Break the 49ers' grip over Santa Clara. Elect these three candidates. (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/31/endorsement-break-the-49ers-grip-over-santa-clara-make-kertes-mayor-elect-inciarte-and-crutchlow-to-council/)
Endorsement: These three City Council candidates are San Jose's best choices (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-peter-ortiz-bien-doan-and-genny-altwer-to-san-jose-city-council/)
Endorsement: Elect Michael Melillo to San Jose Unified School District Board of Education (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-michael-melillo-to-san-jose-unified-school-district-board-of-education/)
Endorsement: Reject San Mateo Community College District’s $848 million Measure V (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-reject-san-mateo-community-college-districts-848-million-measure-v/)
Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
We urge voters to reject it.
Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.

# Prop. 5: Will California voters change the rules for recall elections?
California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms.
Proposition 5 would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office.
If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official.
Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time.
Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024.
It was endorsed by Gov.
Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does Prop. 5 solve?
In its current form, a state-level recall ballot asks two questions in sequence: first, whether to remove an elected official, and second, who should immediately replace them. Although removal requires a majority vote, replacement doesn’t; whoever gets the most votes takes office, even if it’s by a small plurality in a crowded field. That mismatch can mean that an officeholder ousted by majority vote can be replaced by someone with far less support, and it gives well-organized interest groups a powerful incentive to instigate a recall in order to install a preferred candidate who wouldn’t have majority support under normal conditions. Prop. 5 fixes that mismatch by removing the replacement question and filling a vacancy under existing succession law instead.
Related Articles
We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
Why is this the best solution?
Prop. 5 is the best solution because it fixes the specific, politically exploitable flaw — the plurality replacement provision — while still maintaining the recall as a powerful tool of direct democracy. Under its provisions, if a governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor, already duly elected by a majority of Californians statewide, steps in. If a recall takes place in the first two years of the term and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election, voters would still get a special election for a permanent successor, with a runoff if needed to achieve a majority. If the recall takes place later in the term, the lieutenant governor would serve out the remainder of an ousted governor’s term, the same as if they were to leave office for some other reason. In the event of a recall of other state-level officers, those offices would be filled under existing vacancy replacement provisions.
Why would Californians want to remove someone from office but forfeit to the governor their current right to immediately choose a successor?
Two corrections worth making: In the event of a gubernatorial recall, it wouldn’t be the governor who gains power but the lieutenant governor, a separately elected constitutional officer who is, by virtue of California’s Constitution, explicitly and deliberately next in the line of succession. Intrinsic to any lieutenant governor’s campaign is the assertion that he or she is most qualified to step in if events so demand. Second, voters aren’t forfeiting a choice: If a governor is recalled early in their term, Californians would still elect a permanent successor by majority through a special election. This is a sensible change from the current format, where, in the event of a gubernatorial recall, a replacement candidate can become governor of the largest and most important state in the country with only a small plurality, in a special election decided by a reduced electorate in a low-information and highly politicized environment.
Explain how this empowers majority rule and why that matters.
As it currently stands, while recalling a state-level elected official requires majority support, replacing them doesn’t. Only a plurality is required, which could be as low as 20% in a crowded replacement field. Prop. 5 closes that gap. When a successor election is held, if no one wins a majority outright, it would go to a runoff. So, whoever ultimately holds the office would have secured the support of more than half the voters, not just the largest slice of a fractured field. This is the standard California already applies to nearly every other office and election scenario. A recall shouldn’t be the one process where a candidate can take power without the validation of majority voter support.
How does this measure stop political groups from abusing the recall process?
It removes the existing incentive for political gamesmanship at the expense of electoral integrity. As it stands, a well-funded, motivated minority can force a recall and realistically expect its preferred candidate to win the replacement seat with a small plurality, sometimes far fewer votes than the officeholder who was removed. That’s a low bar for a high-value prize, and it’s why some recalls have been criticized as backdoor attempts to grab a seat that couldn’t be won in a regular election. Prop. 5 raises the bar and removes that incentive: Voters will still be able to remove a corrupt or malfeasant official, but it removes the strategic upside of gaming a plurality-only replacement. Instead, a replacement would be made in the normal order, and in the next election, the winner would ultimately secure a majority, with a runoff if needed.
How would this save taxpayers money?
First and foremost, by changing the incentive structure by eliminating the second question, Prop. 5 would save taxpayers money by reducing the likelihood of hyperpartisan recalls like the one which targeted Gov. Prop. 5: Will California voters change the rules for recall elections?

This story was originally published by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/). Sign up (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/) for their newsletters.
California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms.
Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/) would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office. If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time.
Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024. It was endorsed (https://www.abc10.com/article/news/politics/gov-newsom-announces-position-on-statewide-ballot-propositions/103-a92674ac-c53f-46cf-a625-6e469a288eed) by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021.
The outcome of Prop. 5 was far from certain going into Election Day: 45% of people polled in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California said they would vote for it (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/#:~:text=Bay%20Area%20(51%25).-,Proposition%205,-(Changes%20Recall%20Election), while 52% said they wouldn’t. The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes.
Where Prop. 5 came from
In the aftermath of the failed recall of Newsom in 2021, Democratic lawmakers and Secretary of State Shirley Weber began advocating for changes to the process. The Newsom recall effort cost taxpayers about $200 million, and another $100 was spent in the campaign to stop the recall by Newsom’s potential replacements to get their message out to voters. Newsom walked away unscathed, with 62% of voters electing to keep him in office.
Weber and good governance groups argued (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/258090?t=338&f=d2d732fccac5f698c6d6489536c70cb8) the current system leads to unnecessary state expense, confuses voters, and can lead to ‘undemocratic’ outcomes, since the winner needs a plurality of the vote, not the majority, to win.
They supported Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1), authored by Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled himself in 2018. The effort became Prop. 5 when Democratic lawmakers passed it in 2024. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/257408?t=362&f=816848bd63bbdd2078deeadec3321c8c) the reform was not needed, would dilute the power of voters and lead to additional special election costs because of the need to hold two elections.
Unlike some of the tax measures on the ballot that have spurred multimillion-dollar spending sprees, no group has spent any money on the effort, according to CalMatters campaign finance tracker.
Although recalls are often initiated, they rarely make it to voters (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present). Only 11 recalls have made it to the ballot in California since 1913, and only six have been approved by voters. The current recall process is how Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger came into power, replacing Gray Davis in 2003.

California voters will decide on whether the state's recall election process will change.
Proposition 5 could make removing an elected official from office as simple as answering one ballot question. If passed, Prop 5 would remove the current second section, which would mean voters would be asked to elect a sucessor in a separate process.

I'm weighing the recall-replacement clause against the rest: the stated concern is that allowing a removed official to run again undermines the recall's purpose, but voters still decide, so the clause may matter less than the Chronicle suggests. I'm noting that the Little Hoover Commission would also let the most-voted candidate win in a special election, while Prop 5 requires a majority or runoff, so experts don't agree on the fix. I'm weighing the reversibility argument: since a constitutional amendment is hard to undo, a flawed measure whose author can't fully explain its problems is a reasonable reason to vote No. The opposition from the state GOP, several newspapers, and the weak polling all point the same way, though the Legislature's years of effort on this issue cut against that view.

I'm leaning toward "No" for a few reasons: the amendment has an acknowledged drafting flaw its author can't explain, it shifts replacement toward appointment and special elections, and its costs are uncertain. I'm weighing whether the incumbent running in a later special election is really a flaw, since the difference from the snap-election approach is mostly timing and the majority rule. That leaves a real trade-off between majority rule and same-ballot plurality, and I'm not sure which should win.

I'm weighing whether a decision based on expected impact should lean differently, since recalls are rare, so the measure mostly matters in unusual high-stakes cases. I'm weighing whether the partisan split should count against the measure, since all the current statewide offices are held by Democrats and a Democratic governor would make the appointments after a recall. I'm checking the partisan backing and the Senate vote split, which seems to conflict with what I remembered about Republican opposition. I'll set that detail aside rather than chase it, and list the Yes and No considerations in plain terms to see which way they weigh.

I'm leaning toward No on the grounds that the measure bundles several design choices, like the recalled official's eligibility, months-long legislative vacancies, and gubernatorial appointments to other statewide offices, that the rare problem it targets doesn't clearly justify. Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).

Key Takeaways
Nineteen states allow recall of state officials, enabling citizens to remove elected officials before their terms end. Virginia has a process that is similar to recall, but involves a recall trial, where a circuit court determines whether to remove an elected official, rather than an election.
Recall processes vary across states, but generally a recall effort involves collecting a certain number of signatures on a petition within a set timeframe. After a petition meeting the requirements is submitted to the appropriate authority and verified, a recall election is held.
NOTE: The following is presented for informational purposes only. NCSL does not provide advice on how to conduct a recall campaign in any state. For the specific procedures to be followed in any state, please contact your state's election official s (https://www.eac.gov/voters/register-and-vote-in-your-state) .
Introduction
In the 19 states that allow state recall elections, citizens can attempt to remove an elected official from office. Typically, the recall process consists of gathering a certain number of signatures on a petition in a certain amount of time. Beyond this, details of the recall process vary by state. This page explains these processes and provides a list of each state's laws governing the recall of state officials.
Overview
Recall is a procedure that allows citizens to remove and replace a public official before the official’s term of office ends. Historically, recall has been used most frequently at the local level. By some estimates, three-fourths of recall elections are at the city council or school board level. This webpage, however, focuses on the recall only as it applies to state officials.
Recall differs from another method for removing officials from office—impeachment (https://www.ncsl.org/about-state-legislatures/separation-of-powers-impeachment)—in that it is a political device while impeachment is a legal process. Impeachment typically requires a state legislature’s lower chamber to bring specific charges, and the upper chamber to act as the jury in an impeachment trial. In contrast, in most of the 19 recall states specific grounds for recall are not required, and the recall of a state official is accomplished through an election.
Nineteen states plus the District of Columbia permit the recall of state officials:
Alaska – Const. Art. 11, §8; Alaska Stat. §15.45.470-15.45.710
Arizona – Const. Art. 8, Pt. 1, §1-6; Ariz. Rev. Stat.
California – Const. Art 2, §13-19; Cal. Elec. Code §11000-11386
Colorado – Const. Art. 21, Colo. Rev. Stat. §1-12-101 – 1-12-123
District of Columbia – D.C. Code §1-1001.17, §1-204.111 et seq.
Georgia – Const. Art. §2, Para. 4; Ga. Code §21-4-1 et seq.
Idaho – Const. Art. 6, §6; Idaho Code §34-1701 – 34-1715
Illinois – Const. Art. 3, §7
Kansas – Const. Art, 4, §3; Kan. Stat. Ann. §25-4301 – 25-4331
Louisiana – Const. Art. 10, §26; La. Stat. Ann. §18:1300.1 - 18:1300.17
Michigan – Const. Art. 2, §8; Mich. Comp. Laws §168.951 - 168.977
Minnesota – Const. Art. 8, §6; Minn. Stat. Ann. §211C.01 et seq.
Montana – Mont. Code Ann. §2-16-601 – 2-16-635
Nevada – Const. Art. 2, §9; Nev. Rev. Stat. §294A.006, §306.005 et seq.
New Jersey – Const. Art. 1, §2(b); N.J. Rev. Stat. Ann. §19:27A-1 – 19:27A-18
North Dakota – Const. Art. 3, §1 and §10; N.D. Cent. Code §16.1-01-09.1
Oregon – Const. Art. 2, §18; Or. Rev. Stat. §249.865 - 249.877
Rhode Island – Const. Art. 4, §1
Washington – Const. Art. 1, Sec. 33-34; Wash Rev. Code §29A.56.110 - 29A.56.270
Wisconsin – Const. Art. 13, §12; Wis. Stat. Ann. §9.10
All these states lay out the right to recall elected officials in their constitutions, with the exception of Montana, where the right to recall is found only in state statutes. Additionally, each recall state except Illinois and Rhode Island further explains its recall processes in state statutes.
Virginia (https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacodefull/title24.2/chapter2/article7/) has a process that is similar to recall, but it is not listed here as a recall state because its process, while requiring citizen petitions, calls for a recall trial rather than an election (Va. Code Ann. §24.2-233 – 24.2.238). In Virginia, after a petition containing the required number of signatures is verified, a circuit court decides whether a Virginia official will be removed from office. In the recall states, the voters decide in an election. Currently, only these 19 states allow recall elections of statewide elected officials, but other states have considered establishing recall procedures. For state legislative action on recalls and other election topics, reference NCSL’s state elections legislation database (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/state-election-legislation-database) and the archived database (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/state-elections-legislation-archived-database), which has legislation from 2011 to 2024.

History
History and Use of the Recall in the U.S.
The recall device began in the United States in a municipality-Los Angeles-in 1903. Michigan and Oregon, in 1908, were the first states to adopt recall procedures for state officials. Illinois became the most recent state to adopt recall procedures for state officials when voters approved a constitutional amendment in 2010 to allow recall of the governor. Before that, Minnesota (1996) and New Jersey (1993) were the most recent.
Historically, recall attempts at the state level have been largely unsuccessful. The recall is used much more often, and with more success, at the local level.
Many attempts have been made to recall governors throughout U.S. history, but only four have gathered enough petition signatures to trigger recall elections. In 2021, California Gov. Gavin Newsom survived a recall election. In 2012, Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker survived a recall election. In 2003, California voters successfully recalled Gov. Gray Davis, and in North Dakota in 1921, voters successfully recalled not only Gov. Lynn J. Frazier, but also the attorney general and the commissioner of agriculture. In 1988, Arizona voters submitted enough signatures to trigger a recall election for Gov. Evan Mecham, but he was impeached by the state's House of Representatives before the scheduled recall election.
Recall efforts against state legislators are more common, but still unusual. Recall attempts against legislators have gathered enough signatures to trigger an election just 40 times. (Many more recall efforts are started and never make it to the election stage.) Eleven of those occurred in a single year, 2011. Forty-three percent of all legislative recall elections that have ever occurred were held between 2011 and 2013. However, only eight of those 17 elections succeeded in unseating a legislator. Overall, 53% of legislative recall elections have succeeded in unseating a legislator. Additionally, two legislators resigned after petitions with sufficient signatures to force recall elections against them were submitted.

Pros and Cons
Supporters of the recall process believe it provides a way for citizens to exercise control over elected officials who fail to represent their constituents' best interests, or who are unresponsive or incompetent. This view maintains that an elected representative is an agent or a servant of their constituents, not their master.
Opponents argue that recalls can lead to an excess of democracy: That the threat of a recall election lessens the independence of elected officials; undermines the principle of electing good officials and giving them a chance to govern; and can be abused by well-financed special interest groups and give them undue influence over the political process.
Process
How the Recall Process Works
The recall process varies in its details from one state to another, but in general, recall campaigns follow these steps:
File an application to circulate a recall petition (some states allow petitions only if they contain certain grounds for recall (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials#Grounds)).
Circulate a recall petition and gather a specified number of signatures in a specified period of time (view the detailed petitioning requirements (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials#Petition)).
Submit petitions to election officials for verification of signatures.
If enough valid signatures are presented, hold a recall election (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials#Election).
Grounds for Recall
In most of the recall states, any registered voter can begin a recall campaign for any reason. The language in Michigan's constitution is typical of most states: “The sufficiency of any statement of reasons or grounds ... shall be a political rather than a judicial question.” (Mich. Const. Art. II §8) Indeed, recall campaigns are often politically motivated. For example, in 2011, Republican senators in Wisconsin faced recalls for supporting the governor's effort to reduce the influence of public employee unions, and in Arizona, a senator faced recall for sponsoring a controversial immigration bill.
Specific grounds for recall are required in eight states:
Alaska: Lack of fitness, incompetence, neglect of duties or corruption (Alaska Stat. §15.45.510)
Georgia: Act of malfeasance or misconduct while in office; violation of oath of office; failure to perform duties prescribed by law; willfully misused, converted, or misappropriated, without authority, public property or public funds entrusted to or associated with the elective office to which the official has been elected or appointed. Discretionary performance of a lawful act or a prescribed duty shall not constitute a ground for recall of an elected public official. (Ga. Code §21-4-3(7) and 21-4-4(c))
Kansas: Conviction for a felony, misconduct in office or failure to perform duties prescribed by law. Misconduct in office means a violation of law by the officer that impacts the officer’s ability to perform the official duties of the office. No recall submitted to the voters shall be held void because of the insufficiency of the grounds, application, or petition by which the submission was procured. (Kan. Stat. Ann. §25-4302)
Minnesota: Serious malfeasance or nonfeasance during the term of office in the performance of the duties of the office or conviction during the term of office of a serious crime (Minn. Const. Art. VIII, §6).
Montana : Physical or mental lack of fitness, incompetence, violation of oath of office, official misconduct, conviction of certain felony offenses (enumerated in Title 45). No person may be recalled for performing a mandatory duty of the office he holds or for not performing any act that, if performed, would subject him to prosecution for official misconduct. (Mont. Code Ann. §2-16-603)
Rhode Island: Authorized in the case of a general officer who has been indicted or informed against for a felony, convicted of a misdemeanor or against whom a finding of probable cause of violation of the code of ethics has been made by the ethics commission. (R.I. Const. Art. IV, §1)
Virginia: Neglect of duty, misuse of office, or incompetence in the performance of duties when that neglect of duty, misuse of office, or incompetence in the performance of duties has a material adverse effect upon the conduct of the office, or upon conviction of a drug-related misdemeanor or a misdemeanor involving a "hate crime." (Va. Code Ann. §24.2-233)
Washington: Commission of some act or acts of malfeasance or misfeasance while in office, or who has violation of oath of office. (Wash. Const. Art. I §33)
In 2012, Michigan passed a law requiring that a recall petition must clearly and factually state the reason(s) for the recall, which must be based on the elected official's conduct during his or her term of office (Mich. Comp. Laws §168.951A). This differs from the specific grounds required in some other states, as Michigan’s requirement will not necessarily eliminate politically motivated recalls. For example, under this Michigan law a voter could initiate a recall against a legislator on the political grounds that the legislator voted against an issue the voter supports. As long as that allegation is stated clearly and factually, it would presumably meet this new criterion.
Circulating a Recall Petition
The recall process is similar to the ballot initiative process in that it requires the submission of citizen petitions. The number of signatures necessary to trigger a recall election, however, is often significantly higher than the number required for ballot initiatives. The required number of signatures is generally equal to a percentage of the vote in the last election for the office in question, although some states base the formula on the number of eligible voters or other numbers. For instance, in Kansas, “no application for the recall of a state officer may be filed during the first 120 days or last 200 days of the term” of the state officer. Recalls vary based on how the successor is selected:
Seven states hold recall elections simultaneously with election for a successor for most offices: Arizona, California, Colorado, Michigan, Nevada, North Dakota and Wisconsin.
In five states, a recall election is followed by a separate special election for a successor for most state offices: Georgia, Illinois, Louisiana, Minnesota and Rhode Island (state legislature only).
In eight states, a successor is appointed to fill a vacancy created by a recall election: Alaska, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island (offices of secretary of state, attorney general and state treasurer) and Washington.

The Recall Election
Recalls vary based on how the successor is selected:
Seven states hold recall elections simultaneously with election for a successor for most offices: Arizona, California, Colorado, Michigan, Nevada, North Dakota and Wisconsin.
In five states, a recall election is followed by a separate special election for a successor for most state offices: Georgia, Illinois, Louisiana, Minnesota and Rhode Island (state legislature only).
In eight states, a successor is appointed to fill a vacancy created by a recall election: Alaska, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island (offices of secretary of state, attorney general and state treasurer) and Washington.
In some instances, filling vacancies created by recalls differs by office. Ten states—Alaska, Idaho, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Montana, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island and Washington— fill most state-level recall vacancies through special elections or appointment, but the office of governor is filled by the line of succession. Rhode Island uses both the special election and appointment methods, depending on the office. State legislative recall elections are followed by a separate special election for a successor. For the offices of secretary of state, attorney general and state treasurer, recall vacancies are filled by appointment.

The Recall Election
Recalls vary based on how the successor is selected:
Seven states hold recall elections simultaneously with election for a successor for most offices: Arizona, California, Colorado, Michigan, Nevada, North Dakota and Wisconsin.
In five states, a recall election is followed by a separate special election for a successor for most state offices: Georgia, Illinois, Louisiana, Minnesota and Rhode Island (state legislature only).
In eight states, a successor is appointed to fill a vacancy created by a recall election: Alaska, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island (offices of secretary of state, attorney general and state treasurer) and Washington.
In some instances, filling vacancies created by recalls differs by office. Ten states—Alaska, Idaho, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Montana, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island and Washington— fill most state-level recall vacancies through special elections or appointment, but the office of governor is filled by the line of succession. Rhode Island uses both the special election and appointment methods, depending on the office. State legislative recall elections are followed by a separate special election for a successor. For the offices of secretary of state, attorney general and state treasurer, recall vacancies are filled by appointment.
Below is a chart detailing how recall elections are conducted and how a vacancy created by a recall election is filled for state offices. This chart does not cover how judicial vacancies are filled in states where judicial officers may be recalled.

**Yes**, narrowly. It's a close call and partly a values question.

- **Current rules can seat a minority winner.** In 2018, Newman's replacement won with 31.8% of the votes on the recall question, while 41.9% voted to keep him. In 2003, Schwarzenegger won with 46.8% of that vote. Prop 5 would instead fill a recall vacancy through a special election that needs a majority (with a runoff if no one gets one), through succession by the statewide-elected lieutenant governor (for a recalled governor), or through the governor's appointment, which needs legislative confirmation or takes effect automatically after 90 days.
- **The costs and gaps are real but modest.** A recalled legislator's seat would typically stay empty four to five months unless the election is consolidated with another one, and the recalled official could run again in that special election. The Legislative Analyst calls the net cost unknown. Prop 5 also doesn't change what the recall election itself costs.
- **Vote No if** you want the replacement chosen on the same ballot, or you find the vacancy gap or the rerun provision disqualifying. The title ("Statewide Officers") also understates the scope, since legislators are covered too.

The latest PPIC poll (Oct. 16–22) had it at 45% yes and 52% no. The campaign split is largely partisan, and polls close at 8 p.m. on Nov. 3.
